Complete Your first simulation before choosing a task. Each group below leads to implemented guides and checked particle stages.
Group Tasks Data model Model entities and components. Systems and kernels Declare kernel access, order systems, and inspect entities. Structural changes Create and change batches with scoped selections. Resources Share values with resources. Execution Select host/device, pass captures, bind portable resources, run host chunks, reuse device copies, and coordinate shared output. Spatial locality Classify particles, maintain placement explicitly, and select exact clusters. Performance Validate work, profile dominant systems, and measure complete steps. The earlier systems, resource operations, spatial clustering, synchronization, and benchmark pages remain accessible. Use compatibility and status for experimental limits and errors and migration for diagnostics.

Adding and removing individual entities is done via the add_entity and remove_entity methods of World.storage. Revisiting our earlier example of a world with Position and Velocity, this reads as follows:
The examples in this chapter mutate a World directly to demonstrate its storage API. This is useful for setup and isolated changes. In application logic, these operations should generally be performed by a system through its SystemContext.
from larecs import World, Filter, SystemContext, KernelContext @fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): var x: Float64 var y: Float64 @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable): var dx: Float64 var dy: Float64 def place_batch(rows: KernelContext[Filter().include[Position]()]): """Places each execution-local row one unit farther along the x axis.""" for row in rows: row.get[Position]().x = Float64(row.idx) def main() raises: var world = World[Position, Velocity]() # Add an entity and get its representation var entity = world.storage.add_entity() # Remove the entity world.storage.remove_entity(entity) Components can be added to the entities directly upon creation. For example, to create an entity with a position at (0, 0) and a velocity of (1, 0), we can do the following:
entity = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 0))
data.batch-addition#Batch addition:
Systems create batches through add_entities. The result is a movable, noncopyable EntitySelection containing exactly the new rows and owning the world’s structural-change lock:
var context = SystemContext(world) var created = context.add_entities( Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 0), count=10 ) created.run[place_batch]() created^.release() place_batch sets each x to row.idx. The index restarts at zero for each selected host range, so it is not unique across the batch.
Use a with block to release the lock automatically, including when an error or early return exits the block:
with context.add_entities(Position(0, 0), count=10) as selected: selected.add(Velocity(1, 0)) selected.run[place_batch]() selected.run[place_batch]() # The structural lock is released here. For an existing selection, write with selection^ as selected: to transfer ownership into the manager. The bound selection cannot escape the block’s manager. The manager retains the lock until exit, even if the bound selection is consumed or explicitly released inside the block.
Note
A selection can run kernels repeatedly. Component-changing methods update its membership in place and retain the same lock; they return nothing. Call selection^.release() when finished, or let it be destroyed. While it lives, unrelated creation, deletion, and archetype changes are rejected. An empty selection is still locked and follows the same rule.
The lower-level HostStorage.add_entities remains available for setup code, and returns iteration.LockedEntityRange (also named by the HostStorage.Iterator type alias). It borrows storage and its lock manager, records exact bounded batch rows, and supports len, Bool, iteration, and mutable unsafe_get access. Copies share membership metadata but retain independent cursor positions and structural locks; moves transfer the existing lock. Exhaustion, including an empty result, retains the lock until destruction. Use SystemContext.add_entities and a selection kernel for system logic; a storage range has no .run, .add, .remove, or .release method.
The beta concrete return type LockedWorldEntityIterator was renamed to LockedEntityRange; explicit HostStorage.Iterator specializations use has_ranges=True instead of has_start_indices=True. Inferred storage loops need no change. See decision 0022.
data.batch-removal#Batch removal:
If we want to remove multiple entities at once, we need to characterize which entities we mean. To that end, we use queries, which characterize entities by their components. For example, removing all entities that have the component Position can be done with remove_entities as follows:
# Remove all entities that have a Position component world.storage.remove_entities[Filter().include[Position]()]() More on queries can be found in the chapter Queries and iteration.
Tip
Prefer the batch operations when you add or remove many entities. add_entities looks up the target archetype once and grows its columns once for the whole batch, while add_entity repeats both steps per entity. remove_entities clears each matching archetype as a whole instead of removing its rows one at a time. How much this saves depends on the batch size and on the component types.

The focused entity_selection_benchmark.mojo workload compares ordinary full-world host execution with contiguous and disjoint 64-row selections in a 100,000-row world, a selected add/remove chain, and selected device execution when an accelerator is available. On the Apple Metal development host used for the 1.0.0b2 work, one bounded run measured approximately 0.0253 ms for the 100k-row host path, 0.0000664 ms for the contiguous selection, 0.000556 ms for 64 disjoint single-row ranges, 0.00727 ms for the add/remove chain, and 0.379 ms for the device selection. These are development measurements, not a cross-version historical baseline; use the benchmark on target hardware for regression decisions.
The manual host thread dispatch experiment compares complete sequential kernel calls with dynamically claimed whole-store and contiguous chunk jobs at 1/2/4 worker tasks, including small and large increment/compute workloads and single-store cases. Its driver, timing boundaries, reproduction commands, and Linux measurements are recorded there. It is a restricted feasibility benchmark; the current experimental engine adds eligibility and lifecycle checks absent from that prototype. Both drivers remain outside the normal PR performance gate.
data.benchmark-methodology#Benchmark methodol:
Build a focused manual driver once with pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/<benchmark_filename>.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-benchmark, then run /tmp/larecs-benchmark repeatedly. Run the complete manual suite with pixi run mojo run -I src benchmark/run_benchmarks.mojo.
When changing storage, queries, classification, row movement, or execution costs, add or update representative benchmarks using these criteria:
Keep the combined PR performance checks near one minute per runner, including compilation, warmup, and sampling. Measure cold compilation and execution separately on Linux and macOS before expanding the suite. Keep large worlds, GPU cases, and the complete benchmark registry in focused manual drivers. Use deterministic inputs, bounded calibration or fixed iteration counts, and a compact scenario matrix. Spatial cases should cover uniform, dense, sparse, and moving entities with different maintenance cadences. Compare identical entities and semantic work, with an unchanged-layout control. Measure isolated operations and complete frames when useful. Include input updates, classification, sorting, movement, location repair, and transfers whenever they belong to the claimed workload. State excluded setup and maintenance costs; validate results, locations, and payload preservation outside the timer, and consume results to prevent dead-code elimination. Build each timing binary once, then run it repeatedly. Compare the same current driver against baseline and current libraries on the same runner with matching compiler versions and optimization settings. Use optimized builds without debug info, sanitizers, or tracing. Run builds and measurements sequentially, with no competing benchmark jobs, and report compilation separately. Warm both binaries, alternate baseline/current order, and use repeated paired samples. Keep machine-specific timing baselines out of the repository. See PR performance checks and spatial checks for baseline selection, thresholds, confirmation, and support for revisions predating the spatial API. Keep the small regression checks in pixi run tests test on Linux and macOS; focused test-file runs omit performance checks. Investigate sustained failures and document evidence before changing thresholds; use dedicated measurements for smaller regressions. Keep scenario matrices and expected-case manifests synchronized. Invalid or incomplete reports, build failures, and correctness failures must fail checks. Update this guide when changing cases, timing boundaries, sampling, or baseline selection. Record hardware, compiler, method, and limitations with performance claims; track unmeasured benefits and remaining work in the roadmap.
data.deferred-dirty-classification#Deferred d:
Build pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/dirty_spatial.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-dirty-spatial, then run that binary with no concurrent compilation or benchmark jobs. It constructs identical scrambled 2,048/32,768-entity worlds with 72 component bytes per row plus entity IDs, establishes initial spatial order, warms both paths, and alternates five paired samples of sixteen frames (1,024 frames for clean boundaries to resolve their small cost). The 24 scenarios cover uniform (16 entities/cell), dense (256/cell), and sparse (16/cell with key gaps of 128) distributions, with 0, 1, 1/64, or all identities updated. Each updated identity receives two reference writes per frame; classification observes final values. On alternating frames those writes cancel. Other frames advance cells by one. Both paths perform identical updates and semantic work.
The deferred path uses automatic tracking. Its control requests a full rebuild after those same writes. Timings include updates, marking, key scratch allocation, classification, sorting, typed movement of all columns, and location repair. Construction, registration, initial maintenance, and correctness checks are excluded. Every sample validates complete key order, each identity/location, the expected final input for every identity, and all eight payload lanes outside timing through read-only queries. Output records rows, distribution, dirty count, pair number, and deferred/full frame ns. This compares current deferred maintenance with current explicit full rebuilds; it does not measure a historical implementation or total application speedup.
Clean calls do no row work. Dirty calls still copy O(entity-ID capacity) keys and inspect affected archetypes, so sparse classification is not O(D) complete maintenance. Full rebuilds currently reset sparse membership and caches. Dense updates may favor contiguous full classification; structural-heavy workloads use full rebuilds. Retained keys/membership cost at least nine bytes per allocated ID plus queue capacity (full ID/generation identities and allocator slack). Scratch and movement metadata add temporary memory. These are layout costs, not measured application memory usage.
A local run on Apple M4, arm64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567) with implementation 76868ef (based on 0241e91) built the optimized driver in 4.74 seconds. Five warmed pairs gave these median complete-frame times for 32,768 entities:
Distribution Dirty identities Deferred Explicit full rebuild Deferred/full Uniform 1 0.685 ms 1.076 ms 0.637 Uniform 512 0.749 ms 1.133 ms 0.661 Dense 512 0.811 ms 1.194 ms 0.679 Sparse 1 0.097 ms 0.490 ms 0.198 Sparse 512 0.112 ms 0.497 ms 0.226 Uniform 32,768 0.850 ms 0.858 ms 0.991 Across both sizes and all distributions, nonzero sparse-update scenarios took 19.5–67.9% of the full-rebuild frame time. Clean boundaries measured approximately 3–4 ns (close to timer resolution), versus 0.031/0.490 ms full rebuilds at the two sizes. Fully dirty frames took 99.1–104.6% of the explicit control. An earlier version that resolved every dirty identity separately took 131–141% for fully dirty frames; the accepted all-ID-dirty fallback avoids that column/location setup cost. Neither path can avoid moving clean rows when regrouping demands it.
The separate same-driver PR gate against 0241e91 passed all 12 core and 32 spatial cases in 41.1 seconds including four sequential compilations and five paired samples. It found no confirmed regression under the existing 30%/500 ns rule. It still measured approximately 15–19% overhead for reversing maintenance, 10–14% for maintained mobile frames, and 3–8% for ordinary stable-ID access. Those costs remain visible tradeoffs, not claims of zero regression. Linux evidence comes from the PR checks; actual GPU execution is validated separately and is not included in these CPU performance numbers.
data.partitioned-storage-comparison#Partition:
Build the optimized standalone driver once: pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/partitioned_spatial.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-partition-benchmark. Run that binary without concurrent compilation or benchmark jobs. Partitioning is explicitly selected at registration; the control is the same current library’s deferred row reordering, not forced full classification or a historical library with different invalidation costs. The existing core/spatial PR gate separately measures changes to the default paths against the exact base.
The driver constructs identical deterministic scrambled 2,048/32,768-row worlds with two component-defined archetypes, 64-byte SIMD payloads, an integer input, and an additional eight-byte column on half the rows. It compares one growable store per logical cluster with row reordering for uniform (16 identities per cell), dense (1,024 per cell), and singleton sparse (one identity per cell, key spacing 128) distributions. Each configuration warms both layouts with one sixteen-frame batch, then alternates their order for five paired sixteen-frame samples.
The 48 scenarios cover maintenance with 1, 1/64, or all identities updated; ordinary read-only query scans and host execution with unchanged layouts; and complete cell frames with the same updates, maintenance every frame (or every fourth frame for 1/64 updates), all-lane per-cell aggregation, and cyclic adjacent-cell aggregate products. Both layouts use identical entities, input updates, and semantic work. The scan controls still call the clean boundary. All measured update frames include marking, pending key allocation/copy, classification, directory construction or sorting, column growth/movement, source swap-removal, location repair, and allocation reclamation as applicable. Cell frames also include query setup, cell scratch allocation, aggregation, and neighbor arithmetic. Construction, initial placement, policy/device setup, and validation are excluded. There are no device transfers in these CPU timings.
Every sample checks all identities once, final inputs, all payload lanes, entity locations, default key order or homogeneous cluster stores, and equal complete spatial checksums outside timing. Query/host scan reductions are also checked against their complete expected sums. Results are consumed inside the timer. This is a synthetic spatial workload, not a game/simulation speedup, collision detection, or a persistent neighbor index.
MEMORY records report initial maintained capacity-derived owned bytes; MEMORY_AFTER_MOVEMENT reports retained buffers after 96 fully moving frames: physical-directory slots, component/ID buffers, entity locations, key/dirty caches, queued identities, and recycled-slot capacity. Counted allocations are physical-directory plus row-column/ID allocations. Graph/pool allocations, allocator overhead, device state, classifier configuration, and all temporary maintenance/query/cell scratch are excluded; these records are not RSS or peak memory measurements. The components are trivial and have no hidden payload heap. Columns in a store share capacity, but each column and the IDs allocate separately. PAIR records give rows, distribution, mode, update count, cadence, pair index, reordering ns/frame, and partition ns/frame.
Growable-store comparison on Linux The same current driver was built against committed base df0e6c5638beaab2bf3784a2b4784044a7c2707e (256-row-capped blocks) and the growable-store implementation from decision 0014. This local run used AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U, Linux 7.2.5-3-omarchy x86_64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), normal optimized builds without tracing, sanitizers, or debug information. Cold builds ran sequentially and took 11.13 s / 11.11 s (base/current). No other builds or benchmark jobs ran during timing; background desktop services remained active. Five pairs of fresh binary invocations alternated base/current order. Each invocation used the warmup, five paired sixteen-frame samples per case, timing boundaries, and complete validation described above. Values below are medians of the five per-invocation medians, in milliseconds. All 48 cases validated in all ten invocations. Median complete driver execution including validation was 13.10 s / 11.33 s (base/current).
Driver SHA-256: 37795c49baa95f1b911d43327d413097b85a5f60f92f3137accf7abfa9a90ad9.
Distribution Timed work, 32,768 rows Capped blocks Growable stores Growable / capped Uniform Maintenance, 512 updates/frame 0.416 0.256 0.61 Dense Maintenance, 512 updates/frame 0.111 0.072 0.65 Dense Complete frame, all moving 6.032 4.295 0.71 Singleton sparse Complete frame, all moving 20.400 17.231 0.84 Dense Ordinary query scan, clean 0.430 0.427 0.99 Dense Ordinary CPU scan, clean 0.030 0.031 1.03 Uniform Ordinary CPU scan, clean 0.068 0.070 1.03 Singleton sparse Ordinary CPU scan, clean 0.337 0.344 1.02 Dense initial placement used 64 stores and 225 counted allocations, versus 128 blocks and 449 allocations in the base. Initial counted owned bytes fell from 4,448,265 to 4,403,209. After 96 fully moving frames, growable dense stores retained 7,847,945 bytes and 64,512 row slots, versus 5,062,665 bytes and 32,768 slots for capped blocks. Destination stores can grow while their old rows are still awaiting transfer, and nonempty stores retain that spare capacity. Fewer stores therefore do not guarantee less retained memory. These remain capacity-derived buffer measurements, with the exclusions described above.
Full scans changed by -0.8% to +4.3% across these distributions; small timing differences on this desktop runner do not establish a scan improvement. Maintenance and fully moving frame results favor growable stores here, but singleton clusters still have separate allocations and substantial traversal overhead. This is CPU-only synthetic evidence; macOS, GPU, application, peak memory, and additional component-width comparisons remain on the roadmap. Local raw reports are retained under output/performance/growable_clusters/.
Historical bounded-block comparison on macOS The measurements below are historical evidence for decision 0013’s 256-row-capped blocks, not timings for the current growable-store layout. Dense clusters now use fewer stores; sparse clusters still require separate allocations. Rerun the driver before making performance claims about the new layout.
A local optimized run on Apple M4, macOS 27.0.1 arm64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), implementation f3d99cd (base 6037850), built in 7.59 seconds and completed execution/validation in 8.88 seconds. Driver SHA-256: da005387b10958c875771cdfb16cebbe455aa7e883631ef36f021734f355a787. No concurrent builds or benchmark jobs ran. Representative medians across five warmed pairs for 32,768 rows were:
Distribution Timed work Updates / cadence Reordering Partitions Partition / reorder Uniform Maintenance 1 / every frame 0.626 ms 0.336 ms 0.54 Uniform Maintenance 512 / every frame 1.334 ms 0.381 ms 0.29 Dense Maintenance 1 / every frame 0.600 ms 0.017 ms 0.03 Dense Maintenance 512 / every frame 1.348 ms 0.096 ms 0.07 Uniform Complete cell frame 512 / every fourth frame 0.627 ms 0.393 ms 0.63 Dense Complete cell frame 512 / every fourth frame 0.651 ms 0.293 ms 0.45 Uniform Complete cell frame All / every frame 1.956 ms 2.785 ms 1.42 Dense Complete cell frame All / every frame 1.881 ms 3.125 ms 1.66 Singleton sparse Complete cell frame All / every frame 1.357 ms 17.011 ms 12.54 Uniform Ordinary query scan Clean 0.149 ms 0.175 ms 1.17 Dense Ordinary query scan Clean 0.149 ms 0.148 ms 0.99 Singleton sparse Ordinary query scan Clean 0.149 ms 0.237 ms 1.59 Uniform Ordinary host scan Clean 0.019 ms 0.045 ms 2.36 Dense Ordinary host scan Clean 0.019 ms 0.022 ms 1.16 Singleton sparse Ordinary host scan Clean 0.020 ms 0.155 ms 7.92 Initial maintained capacity and allocation evidence for those worlds:
Layout / distribution Counted owned bytes Counted row/directory allocations Partition blocks Row capacity / live rows Reordering, all distributions 4,359,561 8 0 32,768 / 32,768 Partitions, uniform 7,241,737 14,337 4,096 32,768 / 32,768 Partitions, dense 4,448,265 449 128 32,768 / 32,768 Partitions, singleton sparse 27,426,825 114,689 32,768 32,768 / 32,768 All initial blocks were fully occupied at their allocated capacities. Component capacity alone therefore understates partition overhead: physical-store metadata and many separate allocations matter, especially for singleton clusters. At 2,048 rows counted bytes were 273,801 for reordering versus 452,617 uniform, 278,025 dense, and 1,714,185 singleton partition storage. After 96 fully moving frames, counted retained bytes were 4,883,849 for reordering versus 10,116,809 uniform, 5,062,665 dense, and 51,019,785 singleton partitions at 32,768 rows. Uniform partition row capacity grew to 58,320; dense/singleton row capacity remained 32,768. Empty blocks released their row allocations, while partial block growth and high-water directory/queue capacity remained. These are retained-buffer measurements, not peak memory.
Small dense/uniform updates took less elapsed maintenance time with partitions, while directory rebuilding and per-block scans dominated singleton cases. The benchmark measures total elapsed costs, not byte-movement counters. Fully moving workloads were slower despite local transfer. Keep partitions opt-in, and retain the reordering default. The measured bounded-block implementation copied identity-capacity keys, inspected blocks, and could move unchanged rows during same-cluster compaction. The current layout retains key copying and directory scans but removes cross-block compaction; destination growth can still relocate existing columns. Cluster selection scans metadata. Application workloads, other component widths, structural-heavy frames, Linux comparative timings, process/peak memory, and device timings remain on the roadmap. GPU functional integration ran on the actual local accelerator; it is separate evidence from these CPU performance measurements.
The separate default-path PR gate against 6037850 passed all twelve core and 32 spatial cases in 49.2 seconds, including four sequential builds and five paired samples. It required no regression confirmation. Ordinary 2,048-row query/host execution changes were +0.1%/-0.6%, stable-ID access was +3.9%, and selected mutation was +0.9% in that run. These small shared-machine differences are not a zero-overhead guarantee; the existing 30%/500 ns rule is unchanged. Hosted Linux/macOS evidence is retained by the PR checks.
data.pr-to-pr-performance-checks#PR-to-PR per:
pixi run performance-check --base <revision> compares the current library with another Git revision on the same machine. Without --base, local runs compare the working tree against committed HEAD; GitHub PR runs use the exact PR base SHA, and main-branch push runs use the previous push commit. The tested current revision is the checkout SHA (normally the PR merge commit in CI). The complete pixi run tests test command runs the gate on Linux and macOS following correctness tests. Focused test-file runs omit it.
The coordinator builds the same current driver against both source trees with the installed Mojo compiler, using optimized builds without tracing, debug information, or sanitizers. It warms both binaries, then runs five pairs, alternating baseline/current order. A case becomes a candidate only if four pairs and the paired medians show over 30% slowdown and over 500 ns extra operation/frame time. Candidates are checked in a fresh five-pair round; only candidates recurring in both rounds fail. Invalid/incomplete reports, incorrect results, compilation failures, unavailable baselines, and timeouts fail rather than silently skipping coverage.
The two focused drivers avoid the expensive complete benchmark registry:
Core case Sizes Timed work Excluded setup and validation access 512/2,048 matching rows Stable-ID component reads and integer checksum World construction; exact per-entity payload checks query 512/2,048 matching rows Fresh filtered iterator, row visits, and checksum Construction of two matching archetypes and equally many excluded tag-only rows; payload checks execute 512/2,048 rows Ordinary host dispatch and integer increments Construction; check every row’s accumulated increments selected_execute 64 selected rows amid 512/2,048 background rows Host dispatch over a reusable contiguous selection Construction and selection creation/release; selected and untouched-row checks selected_mutation Same selection/background sizes Add/remove a tag, including partial-archetype movement and location repair Construction; final membership, absence of tags, payload, and background-location checks batch_cycle 512/2,048 rows Batch creation, payload initialization, removal, and recycling World construction and first validation/warmup cycle; recycled payload, membership, and surviving control-row checks Core calibration doubles from 8 to at most 8,192 operations, stopping at 5 ms per case. Fast cases can reach the cap first. Each duration is per complete operation, not per entity. Read cases consume the checksum inside the timer; execution writes are checked after timing, with observable lengths consumed inside the timer. Spatial boundaries and its unchanged matrix are below.
Run one driver with pixi run core-benchmarks or pixi run spatial-benchmarks. Select a gate with pixi run performance-check --suite core --base <revision> or --suite spatial; repeat --suite to select multiple drivers. The original pixi run spatial-performance-check remains a spatial-only compatibility command.
Reports default to the ignored output/performance/ directory; use --output to choose another directory. report.json includes the schema version, requested/resolved/effective baselines, current checkout SHA and dirty state, driver SHA-256 hashes, compiler, OS/CPU, thresholds, compilation and sampling costs, all paired measurements, and both confirmation rounds when needed. summary.md gives median times, paired changes, candidates, and confirmed failures. Candidates whose confirmation did not finish are labeled unconfirmed; only a completed confirmation can label a candidate transient. Process logs retain build, warmup, execution, and error diagnostics. GitHub adds the Markdown to the job summary and uploads the reports/logs as performance-<runner>-<attempt> artifacts for 30 days, including failed checks. This uses read-only PR permissions and works without publishing PR comments. Require the existing build/test checks in branch protection to enforce the gate.
The initial unchanged-library comparison against 688fb67 on Apple M4, macOS 27 arm64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), took 55.3 seconds: core builds 9.3/9.6 seconds and sampling 2.6 seconds; spatial builds 5.8/5.4 seconds and sampling 22.2 seconds. Builds and samples ran sequentially; no concurrent builds or benchmark jobs ran. These are driver compilation costs in an already installed environment, not dependency installation time.
The first hosted run compared the same unchanged library against 688fb67, using PR merge checkout ba8b180, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), the same current driver on each side, fresh output binaries, sequential compilation/sampling, and five alternating pairs. Both suites passed without confirmation, and both artifact uploads succeeded:
Runner CPU / OS All driver builds All sampling Total gate macos-latest Apple M2 Pro (Virtual), macOS 26.6.2 arm64 43.1 s 22.1 s 66.1 s ubuntu-latest AMD EPYC 7763, Linux 6.17 x86_64 / glibc 2.39 50.2 s 24.6 s 75.3 s These are one-run runtime measurements, not speed comparisons between platforms or evidence that the runner’s load is stable. Full correctness tests, examples, package checks, and environment installation are excluded from these gate costs. The combined check stays near a minute; further coverage requires new budget measurements on both platforms. Confirmation adds sampling cost for affected suites; command deadlines bound failures rather than promising a one-minute runtime for all error/confirmation paths.
There are no checked-in machine-specific golden timings. Driver changes affect both sides; compare historical evidence only when hashes and environments are compatible. Compiler upgrades do not measure compiler-to-compiler changes. These broad thresholds target substantial regressions on shared runners; smaller or cumulative regressions, larger worlds, heap-backed payloads, disjoint selections, and device costs need focused measurements or future coverage. See decision 0011 and the roadmap.
data.resource-execution#Resource execution:
resource_execution_benchmark.mojo uses the current execution API. Compare the same workload against the base library, adapting only backend call spelling when the base predates ExecutionBackend. It measures complete calls over 512 Int32 rows with either no resources or one legacy scalar resource. resource_adapter_benchmark.mojo measures current read-only adapters over the same rows and 4,096 initial Int32 samples. Only the first sample is read; the entire source is uploaded. Each timed adapter call edits that sample, and growth cases append one sample per call. Host calls use 10,000 iterations; GPU calls use 100. One warmup invocation precedes each timer. Construction and final checks are excluded; validation, leases, component transfers, resource uploads/downloads, allocation growth, and synchronization are included when applicable. Exact outputs, row counts, source values, and final sample lengths are checked outside timing.
Copy the current driver for the baseline build:
cp benchmark/resource_execution_benchmark.mojo /tmp/resource_base.mojo If the base accepts on_device: Bool rather than backend: ExecutionBackend, adapt only that copy before compiling it:
python - <<'PYCODE' from pathlib import Path import re path = Path("/tmp/resource_base.mojo") source = path.read_text().replace(" ExecutionBackend,\n", "") source, count = re.subn( r"backend=\(\s*ExecutionBackend\.DEVICE if device else ExecutionBackend\.HOST\s*\)", "on_device=device", source, ) assert count == 4, "Review the driver before adapting a changed call matrix" assert "ExecutionBackend" not in source.split('from std.time', 1)[1] path.write_text(source) PYCODE This maps the same compile-time device boolean to the older keyword; kernels, row counts, iterations, warmup, validation, and timing boundaries stay identical. Do not substitute a historical driver with different workloads. Device comparisons require a working accelerator on both sides; an older host fallback is not a device measurement. For a base using on_gpu, use that keyword instead.
Build optimized binaries once without debug information, sanitizers, or tracing:
pixi run mojo build -I /path/to/base/src /tmp/resource_base.mojo -o /tmp/resource-base pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/resource_execution_benchmark.mojo -o /tmp/resource-current pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/resource_adapter_benchmark.mojo -o /tmp/resource-adapters On Apple M4, macOS 27.0.1, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), compare base 6a3841b against this implementation with the same driver. Warm each binary, then run five paired samples, alternating base/current order, with no concurrent compilation or benchmark jobs. Median per-call means were:
Complete invocation Base Current Host, no resource 294.2 ns 299.6 ns Host, legacy scalar resource 299.8 ns 350.7 ns GPU, no resource 250.50 µs 251.52 µs GPU, legacy scalar resource 243.51 µs 268.59 µs Host, edited adapter — 449.1 ns Host, edited adapter plus growth — 451.4 ns GPU, edited adapter — 323.76 µs GPU, edited adapter plus growth — 303.54 µs The scalar GPU case costs about 10.3% more with staged publication and lifetime protection. These measurements establish the cost of this synthetic workload, not an application speedup or Tree-D shading result. Short GPU batches are noisy; the growth-case ordering does not establish a growth benefit. Source/sample allocation and scientific preprocessing during initial construction are excluded; incremental host append and device allocation growth are included in growth cases. Existing allocation capacity is reused in nongrowing cases; contents are uploaded every run.
Sequential base/current/adapter driver builds took 1.18/3.00/3.01 seconds with existing compiler caches and no competing builds. These are recorded build costs, not comparable cold-compilation measurements. Linux resource timings and cold compilation remain unmeasured. These focused manual cases do not enlarge the normal PR performance matrix.
data.shared-host-execution-comparison#Shared:
The focused selection driver also measures thin and lexical host kernels over seven matching archetypes (512 rows each) alongside six nonmatching archetypes (512 rows each). All matching rows perform the same increment; the closure also counts range invocations. Construction and result checks are excluded, and checks outside the timer verify row count, every row against Bencher.num_iters, and the closure’s exact invocation count and accumulated values. These cases remain manual benchmarks; they are not added to the small PR suite.
On Apple M4, macOS 27.0.1, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), the shared host setup refactor in 1cd32ba was compared with 688fb670c87ced6b08c920e2c3527a1890218c6f using the same updated driver and compiler environment. Build one optimized binary against an isolated baseline checkout and one against the current source, without -g, sanitizers, or tracing. Warm each once, then alternate baseline/current order across five paired samples with no concurrent builds or benchmark jobs. The driver uses fixed iterations: 100 full-world calls, 1,000 multi-archetype calls, 10,000 contiguous selected calls, and 1,000 disjoint selected calls.

data.small-spatial-benchmarks-on-every-pr#Sma:
Run pixi run spatial-benchmarks for one bounded CPU-only comparison, or pixi run spatial-performance-check --base <revision> for a regression check. The complete pixi run tests test command runs this suite through the shared coordinator after successful correctness tests, on both Linux and macOS PR runners. Focused test-file runs omit it. The existing 100,000-row maintenance benchmark and the full benchmark suite remain manual measurements.
The small driver uses 512 and 2,048 entities, one archetype, an integer cell key and a 128-byte SIMD payload per row. It inserts rows in a deterministic scrambled order, then compares the same stable-ID cell visits before and after spatial ordering. Its 32 cases cover:
Workload Cell distribution Timed work Static cell aggregates Uniform: 8 entities/cell Read keys and all payload lanes; sum and square each cell’s aggregate Static cell aggregates Dense: 64 entities/cell Same operation, with fewer occupied cells Static cell aggregates Sparse: 8 entities/cell, key gaps of 1,024 Same operation across nonconsecutive occupied keys Maintenance alone All three distributions Clean explicit boundary, or reverse keys via stable-ID access and sort/move/repair every pass Moving cell aggregates Uniform Update every entity’s cell, aggregate cells, maintain every frame or every fourth frame Static workload timing excludes construction, registration, and the initial maintenance pass. Mobile timing includes input updates and the selected maintenance cadence; its scrambled control performs the same updates and cell visits without maintenance. Maintenance-only reversal and conservative marking via mutable stable-ID access are included in timing. A clean ordered boundary uses deferred maintenance in the current library and full classification in older baseline libraries. This is an intentional maintenance-contract change; use the dedicated comparison below for an explicit full-scan control. Checksums validate aggregate results and payload preservation, and a query validates maintenance’s output order, outside the timer. These are synthetic cell aggregates; full neighborhood algorithms, additional archetypes, transfer costs, and larger working sets remain separate measurements.
Each batch doubles from 8 to at most 8,192 frames, stopping once it takes 20 ms. The checker compiles the same current driver against the current library and the PR’s base commit, warms both binaries, then collects five paired runs with alternating execution order. It reports median frame times and paired changes for both ordered and scrambled controls. A case fails only when at least four pairs show both over 30% slowdown and over 500 ns extra time, and the paired medians exceed those thresholds. A suspected regression must recur in a fresh five-pair run. This broad threshold catches substantial regressions on shared runners; smaller changes need dedicated measurements. No machine-specific timing baseline is checked in.
The baseline comes from the GitHub PR event’s base SHA. Local runs default to committed HEAD; pass --base to compare another revision. An unavailable full SHA is fetched over public HTTPS. Since release PR #174 predates the spatial API, spatial PR #175 bootstraps against 42234f3b43d4dda58a674842374115f78ec2f08d, the implementation before this benchmark addition. Subsequent PRs whose base has the spatial API use their actual base. Compilation, malformed/missing records, checksum failures, and sustained regressions all fail the check.

Concurrent sibling builds overlapped every sample, so these results support no controlled regression or speedup claim. Query/range metadata sharing is checked directly in the cursor regression tests.
data.synchronization-primitives#Synchronizati:
benchmark/synchronization_benchmark.mojo is a focused manual comparison of 100,000 sequential scalar increments using a plain scalar control, direct Mojo relaxed atomics, Larecs relaxed atomic views, and uncontended write guards. Every case performs equivalent increments and consumes results. Setup and final exact total validation are excluded; guard acquisition, payload access, and release are included. These are isolated uncontended costs, not complete ECS execution, contention, allocation, transfer, or GPU measurements. No new timing cases are added to the normal PR performance suite.
Build once without debug information, sanitizers, or tracing, warm the binary, then run repeated samples without other builds or benchmark jobs:
pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/synchronization_benchmark.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-synchronization /tmp/larecs-synchronization Report compilation time separately from execution and retain hardware/compiler details with timing claims. Concurrent compound access and exact atomic totals are correctness checks in test/synchronization_test.mojo; contended performance and complete binding/transfer measurements remain roadmap work.
data.threaded-host-execution#Threaded host ex:
benchmark/threaded_execution.mojo measures the implemented public SystemContext.run[kernel, threaded=True]() against unchanged sequential calls. Both worlds have identical initial rows, arithmetic, and layout. The driver covers 1/2/4 worker tasks, one/four stores, balanced and seven-to-one skewed stores, 1,024–1,048,576 total rows, and increments or 32 dependent arithmetic rounds per row. It forces min_parallel_rows=0 to expose dispatch overhead; configured one-worker runs still use whole-range sequential fallback.
Each case warms both paths twice, calibrates the sequential path to a 10 ms batch or at most 4,096 calls, then alternates order across five paired samples. Complete-call timing includes discovery, validation, spatial-invalidation checks, resource binding, context allocation, atomic claiming, dispatch, join, cleanup, and world-size consumption. Construction, initial runtime warmup, compilation, and exact result validation are excluded. Every final row is validated against all warmup, calibration, and measured calls. No resources or spatial classifiers are bound; shared-resource, selected, and partitioned correctness lives in the tests, while their performance remains unmeasured here.

Run measurements without other builds or benchmark jobs. Each PAIR line contains skew flag, base rows per store, store count, arithmetic rounds, worker count, pair index, calls per batch, sequential ns/call, and threaded ns/call. In skewed cases, total rows are ten times the base row count. Report compilation separately and retain hardware/compiler details; this synthetic comparison establishes no portable cutoff, fixed speedup, or application-level benefit.

data.versus-array-of-structs#Versus Array of:
The plots below show the iteration time per entity in the classical Position-Velocity example. That is, iterate all entities with components Position and Velocity, and add velocity to position:
position.x += velocity.x position.y += velocity.y The benchmark is performed with different amounts of “payload components”, where each of them has two Float64 fields, just like Position and Velocity. Further, the total number of entities is varied from 100 to 1 million.
The documentation workflow (.github/workflows/publish.yml) regenerates this plot for each published commit on a GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest runner, using the Mojo version pinned in benchmark/plots/pixi.lock. The workflow does not record the runner’s CPU or cache sizes, and the hardware behind that runner label can change between runs. Read the plot as a comparison on one machine, not as a prediction for other hardware. Each run keeps the raw results as its aos-benchmark artifact. data:
Entities may be changed by altering the values / attributes of their components, adding new components, or removing existing components.
This chapter uses the World API directly to demonstrate each operation. In application logic, systems are the principal place for these state changes. A system can access an individual entity through its SystemContext, while updates over all entities matching a filter belong in a kernel.
data.accessing-and-changing-individual-compon:
The values of an entity’s component can be accessed and changed via the get method of World.storage.
from larecs import World, Entity, Filter, Components, SystemContext from std.testing import * @fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): var x: Float64 var y: Float64 @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable): var dx: Float64 var dy: Float64 def main() raises: var world = World[Position, Velocity]() A reference to a component can be obtained as follows:
# Add an entity with a component var entity = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0)) # Get a reference to the position; ref pos = world.storage.get[Position](entity) # We can change the reference. pos.x = 5 assert_equal(world.storage.get[Position](entity).x, 5) # We can also replace the component completely. world.storage.get[Position](entity) = Position(10, 0) assert_equal(world.storage.get[Position](entity).x, 10) Of course, accessing a component only works if the entity has the component in question. Accessing a component that the entity does not have will result in an error.
# Add an entity without a velocity component entity = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0)) with assert_raises(): # This will result in an error _ = world.storage.get[Velocity](entity) We can check if an entity has a component using the has method.
# Check if the entity has a velocity component if world.storage.has[Velocity](entity): print("Entity has a velocity component") else: print("Entity does not have a velocity component")
data.adding-and-removing-components#Adding an:
Components can be added and removed from entities using the add and remove methods.
# Add an entity without components entity = world.storage.add_entity() # Add components to the entity world.storage.add(entity, Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 1)) # Remove a component from the entity world.storage.remove[Velocity](entity) This works with arbitrary numbers of components, so we can add or remove any number of components at once.
If we want to remove some components and replace them with other components directly, we can use the replace method in combination with the by method. The replace method takes Components to be removed as parameters, whereas the by method takes the new components to be added.
# Replace the position component with a velocity component world.storage.replace[Position]().by(Velocity(2, 2), entity=entity) Similar to the add and remove methods, this works with arbitrary numbers of components, so we can replace any number of components with any other number of new components.
Tip
Replacing components in one go is significantly more efficient than removing and adding components separately.
Batch operations Sometimes you need to add or remove components from multiple entities at once. Larecs🌲 provides batch operations that are more efficient than performing individual operations on each entity.
Tip
Batch operations are significantly more efficient than individual operations when working with large numbers of entities, as they minimize memory reorganization and improve cache locality.
Use add, remove, and replace for filtered batch changes. Each returns a locked selection containing only rows actually modified:
var context = SystemContext(world) var created = context.add_entities(Position(0, 0), count=10) created.add[ Velocity, filter=Filter().include[Position].exclude[Velocity]() ](Velocity(1.0, 0.5)) An omitted selection-operation filter means no restriction beyond the saved membership. A supplied filter is intersected with that membership; skipped rows are unchanged and leave the selection’s updated membership. Kernel filter mismatches simply skip rows, but invalid component requests still raise.
created.remove[Velocity]() Selection replacement uses a compile-time Components list for removed types; the replacement value types are inferred from the arguments. This direct form avoids an intermediate builder that would also need to own the lock.
created.replace[ remove=Components[Position](), ](Velocity(2.0, 2.0)) created^.release() Important
Selection component-changing calls mutate the same object and return nothing. Validation errors preserve its membership and lock, so it can be used again. Release it explicitly when finished, or use a with block for cleanup.
data.setting-multiple-components-at-once#Sett:
We can set the values of multiple components at once using the set method. This method takes an arbitrary number of components and sets them all in one go.
# Add an entity with two components entity = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 1)) # Set multiple components at once world.storage.set(entity, Position(5, 5), Velocity(2, 2))

data.declare-the-worlds-component-types#Decla:
Represent each simulated object as an entity and store its per-object values in components. This page uses the particles from Your first simulation.
@fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): """Where a particle is.""" var x: Float64 """Horizontal coordinate.""" var y: Float64 """Vertical coordinate.""" @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable): """How far a particle moves per unit of time.""" var dx: Float64 """Horizontal speed.""" var dy: Float64 """Vertical speed.""" var world = World[Position, Velocity]() world.resources.add(Time(delta=0.1)) var walker = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 0)) var climber = world.storage.add_entity(Position(5, 0), Velocity(0, 2)) var marker = world.storage.add_entity(Position(-3, -3))
Position and Velocity are components. World[Position, Velocity] declares the component types the world can store. Each HostStorage.add_entity call creates an entity with the given components and returns its handle.
Define components A component is a struct that conforms to ComponentType, which requires Copyable and Deinitable. Copyable, Movable satisfies both. An entity holds at most one value of each component type.
A component with no fields is a tag. Its presence carries the information, and filters can require or exclude it like any other component.
Declare the world’s component types World lists every component type at compile time. An entity of World[Position, Velocity] can have either component, both, or neither: in the example, marker has only a Position. Resources live in separate storage and do not appear in this list.
Larecs groups entities with the same set of components into a logical archetype. You need no knowledge of this layout to create entities or run systems over them.
data.keep-entity-handles#Keep entity handles:
An Entity is a copyable ID and generation, not the address of its components. Keep the handle to find the entity again, for example with HostStorage.get.
Removing an entity invalidates its handle. Larecs increments the generation before it reuses the ID, so an old handle never refers to a new entity. A handle belongs to the world that created it. Do not use it with another world. Structural changes can move an entity’s components in memory. Keep the handle across structural changes, not component references or row indices.
data.next-steps#Next steps: Update entities with systems and kernels for repeated simulation work. Create and remove entities in batches for creating many entities at once.

/larecs/pr-preview/pr-241/guide/data_mod.title: Model data with entities and components

data:
Larecs🌲 is an entity component system (ECS) framework for Mojo. The ECS concept is composed of three principal elements:
Entities represent game objects or simulation entities, like individuals in a population model. Components are the data associated to entities, i.e. their properties or state variables. Systems contain the game or simulation logic that reads and mutates ECS state. They use a system context to access the world and to run kernels over filtered sets of components. In an ECS, each entity is “composed of” an arbitrary set of components that can be added and removed at run-time. This modular design enables the development of highly flexible and reusable games or simulations. By decoupling the logic (systems) from the data (entities and components), ECS avoids convoluted inheritance hierarchies and eliminates hard-coded behavior. Instead, entities can be composed of components to exhibit diverse behaviors without sacrificing modularity.
An ECS engine manages this architecture within a central storage structure known as the “World”. The engine handles common tasks such as maintaining entity lists, spawning or deleting entities, and scheduling logic operations, simplifying the development process for users.
Larecs🌲 provides a high-performance ECS framework, empowering developers to create games and simulation models with exceptional flexibility and efficiency.
data.components#Components:
Components are the data associated with entities, characterizing their state and properties. Components are represented via structs: each component type is a different struct. For example, if we want to model a world in which entities may have a position and a velocity, we need to define a Position and a Velocity struct.
@fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): var x: Float64 var y: Float64 @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable): var dx: Float64 var dy: Float64 These structs are not only used to store data. Their types are also used as unique identifiers for the components of an entity. That is, they have a similar role to a key in a dictionary.
How components can be assigned to entities is described in the following chapters.
A component type can be any Copyable & Deinitable struct, including one that owns heap memory, such as a List field. Kernels add requirements for the components they access, depending on where they run:
Execution Requirement for accessed components Sequential host (default) None beyond Copyable & Deinitable Threaded host (experimental) Pointer-free value with trivial copy, move, and destruction Device (experimental) Conforms to TrivialRegisterPassable A kernel that accesses an ineligible component fails to compile. Storage operations and queries accept every component type.
Prefer plain values such as Position and Velocity. When entities change archetype or are removed, Larecs runs the move constructors and destructors of owning components row by row, and such components cannot be used by threaded or device kernels.
data.entities#Entities:
Entities are the central unit around which the data in an ECS is organized. Entities could represent game objects, or potentially anything else that “lives” in a game or simulation. Each entity can possess an arbitrary set of components, which can also be used to characterize an entity. That is, in an ECS, cars would not be directly identified as “cars” but rather as something that has the components Position, Velocity, Fuel reserves, Engine power, etc.
The components are not stored in individual objects but rather in a central container, called the World. Hence, an Entity is merely an identifier that allows retrieving the corresponding components from the world. As such, entities are strictly bound to the world they live in, but also small in memory and easy to store.
Note
Though entities can safely be stored and passed around, their components (or pointers to them) should never be stored externally, as they can move in memory at any time.
How entities are created and used is discussed in the next chapters.
data.the-world#The world:
The central data structure of Larecs🌲 is the World. It stores all data and information about the state of the entities and their surroundings. The World struct provides the main functionality of the ECS, such as adding and removing entities, looking up components, and iterating over entities.
Larecs🌲 gains efficiency and usability by exploiting Mojo’s compile-time programming capabilities. To that end, it needs to know ahead of time which components might turn up in the world, and the World must be statically parameterized with the component types upon creation. This also has the advantage that certain errors can already be prevented at compile time, which makes the program safer and faster.
To set up a World, simply import it from the larecs package and create a World instance as follows:
from larecs import World def main(): # Create a world with the components Position and Velocity var world = World[Position, Velocity]()

Choose how a checked particle kernel receives data and where it runs. Complete Your first simulation and Share time and configuration first. Each guide is an optional, independently runnable stage.
Task Result Execute on a device Select a target explicitly and check its results against host execution. Pass local values to kernels Use lexical host borrows or ordered explicit capture slots. Use portable resources Keep owning collections on the host and bind target-local kernel views. Run threaded host kernels Process independent chunks and verify sequential parity. Reuse unchanged device copies Skip unchanged uploads while preserving eager copy-back. Coordinate shared writes Choose per-row output, single-writer reduction, or supported standalone primitives. Compatibility and status records the development version and experimental boundaries. Errors and migration indexes common failures; each stage gives its own restrictions and recovery steps.

Pass a step-local scale or result without storing it as a world resource. Start with movement and resources. Choose a lexical closure for sequential host borrows, or explicit slots for a thin kernel that can also run on a device. Threaded execution accepts neither capture path; its inputs belong in read-only resources or components.
data.declare-explicit-slots-for-a-thin-kernel:
The alternative stage declares ordered Captures slots, independent of the world’s resource types.
comptime move_filter = Filter().include[Position]().read[Velocity]() comptime move_resources = Resources().read[Time]() comptime locals_spec = Captures[ReadCapture[Float32], MutCapture[Int32]]() def move(context: KernelContext[move_filter, move_resources, locals_spec]): """Moves particles and records the processed count with a single writer. Args: context: Rows, time, and ordered scale/count capture slots. """ ref time = context.resources.get[Time]() var scale = context.captures.get[0]() for particle in context: ref position = particle.get[Position]() ref velocity = particle.get[Velocity]() position.x += velocity.dx * time.delta * scale position.y += velocity.dy * time.delta * scale # The count is shared, not one private scalar per device thread. comptime if is_gpu(): if global_idx.x != 0: return context.captures.get[1]() += context.length Slot 0 is a ReadCapture input; slot 1 is a MutCapture result. get[0] is immutable. The output is shared by all invocations/threads, not private per row. On host, one writer per store adds that store’s length. On device, only global thread zero adds the packed length, after its own row loop. This works because the result does not read other threads’ outputs. It is not a barrier or a general parallel reduction.
Bind locals in exactly the declared order when the system runs.
@fieldwise_init struct Move[backend: ExecutionBackend](System): """Binds local values for one synchronous step.""" def update(mut self, mut context: SystemContext[...]) raises: """Checks count copy-back before the system returns. Args: context: Access to the simulation world. Raises: Error: If binding, execution, or the count check fails. """ var scale: Float32 = 2 var processed: Int32 = 0 context.run[move, backend=Self.backend]( read_capture(scale), mut_capture(processed) ) assert_equal(scale, 2) assert_equal(processed, 37) read_capture and mut_capture borrow their locals until run finishes. Host execution borrows the original values; device execution uploads each binding on every call and copies mutable slots back before return. Empty matches leave captures unchanged. The checked full program also tests an empty world and 37 particles split across two physical stores.
From the repository root, execute this independent stage:
pixi run mojo run -I src examples/particles/captures.mojo The program always checks host execution. Its explicit device PASS line means actual execution and copy-back; a SKIP line means that device validation did not run. Device setup explains availability failures.
data.restrictions-and-recovery#Restrictions a:
Failure or restriction Response Wrong slot count, type, or mutability Match Captures in binding order. Slots may share a type; their index still distinguishes them. Conflicting borrows of one local Use separate values; the borrow checker rejects overlapping read/mutable bindings. Heap owner or host pointer in a device capture Captures transfer trivial bytes, not object graphs, and perform no DevicePassable conversion. Use a portable resource for owned storage. A captured reference outlives execution Keep references and pointers inside the invocation. Neither lexical nor explicit capture references may escape it. Several writers update one output Choose a proven single writer or per-row output and a later reduction. Mutable capture access supplies no synchronization. Device execution remains experimental. Prefer explicit bindings when the same thin kernel must run on both targets; use portable resources when the input persists between steps or owns data.

Args: context: Access to the particle world. Raises: Error: If resources, execution, or the visit check fail. """ var scale: Float32 = 2 var visits = 0 def move( rows: KernelContext[ Filter().include[Position]().read[Velocity](), Resources().read[Time](), ] ) {imm scale, mut visits}: """Moves each row and counts it through a host borrow. Args: rows: One matching physical store's rows and time. """ ref time = rows.resources.get[Time]() for particle in rows: ref position = particle.get[Position]() ref velocity = particle.get[Velocity]() position.x += velocity.dx * time.delta * scale position.y += velocity.dy * time.delta * scale visits += 1 context.run(move) assert_equal(visits, 2) def main() raises: """Checks the closure across two matching physical stores. Raises: Error: If setup, execution, or a position check fails. The driver compares the full mutation sequence, including eager host results, against default device transfers and a host baseline.

data.enable-reuse-and-invalidate-escaped-writ:
The sequence below enables World.reuse_device_copies, reads without invalidating, and then changes resource and component inputs.
def run_stage[backend: ExecutionBackend](reuse: Bool) raises -> Position: """Runs a mutation sequence under one transfer policy. Parameters: backend: Explicit execution target. Args: reuse: Whether unchanged device copies may skip uploads. Raises: Error: If execution or the expected coordinates disagree. Returns: A snapshot of the walker's final position. """ var world = World[Position, Velocity]() world.resources.add(Time(0.25)) var walker = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 2)) world.reuse_device_copies(reuse) var scheduler = Scheduler[Position, Velocity](world^) scheduler.add_system(Move[backend]()) scheduler.initialize() scheduler.update(steps=1) # x = 0.25 _ = scheduler.world.resources.read[Time]().delta _ = scheduler.world.storage.read[Velocity](walker).dx scheduler.update(steps=1) # x = 0.5; read calls preserve reuse scheduler.world.resources.get[Time]().delta = 0.5 scheduler.update(steps=1) # x = 1.0; get advances the resource revision # This pointer survives a later run; subsequent writes bypass tracking. var time_ptr = Pointer(to=scheduler.world.resources.get[Time]()) scheduler.update(steps=1) # x = 1.5 time_ptr[].delta = 1.0 scheduler.world.resources.invalidate_device[Time]() scheduler.update(steps=1) # x = 2.5; explicit invalidation refreshes Time scheduler.world.storage.get[Velocity](walker).dx = 2 scheduler.update( steps=1 ) # x = 4.5; component get advances its column revision scheduler.finalize() var result = scheduler.world.storage.read[Position](walker).copy() assert_almost_equal(result.x, 4.5) assert_almost_equal(result.y, 7.0) scheduler.world.reuse_device_copies(False) return result read and read-only queries preserve reusable copies. get through mutable storage conservatively advances a revision even if you only read it. The pointer obtained before a later run does not trigger tracking when you subsequently write through it. invalidate_device[Time]() after that write forces a refresh. Reacquiring with get after each run is the preferred alternative. Neither invalidation path permits mutation during a live invocation or makes an invalid reference safe.
The data-validity sequence differs from allocation reuse.
Retained capacity does not prove that its contents are current.
The revision labels identify host data states. A current record skips an upload; a changed record requires one. Downloaded outputs become current after successful completion. A revision mismatch does not require discarding a large enough allocation. This also applies to read-only adapted resources: validation and leases still run, but a current copy skips the whole prepare_device hook and reuses its descriptor and samples. Mutable adapters always prepare; explicit captures upload every call.
data.know-which-operations-advance-revisions#: Data Operations that can invalidate reusable bytes Resource Add/set, mutable get, and host/threaded/device runs declaring writable access. Removal discards its records. Component type in a physical store Mutable storage/row access, setters and kernels declaring writes, including exact selected ranges. All columns affected by placement Structural changes, spatial row permutations, partition transfers and store growth/replacement. Escaped references or raw pointers Untracked writes require resource-specific invalidate_device[T]() or World.invalidate_device_copies for all copies. Component reuse also requires the same store incarnation, contiguous row range, packed offset, and revision. Alternating filters or selections can change pack offsets and cause reuploads despite unchanged host values. A world copy starts with independent host owners and empty device records. Disabling reuse clears records; it does not turn completion asynchronous. Failed queued invocations invalidate their touched copies; an unusable world must still be replaced.

Written data still downloads This is required eager copy-back. Measure complete calls, including downloads and synchronization. Measure complete simulation steps before retaining this optimization.

data: Run the particle movement kernel on an explicitly selected accelerator, then check the result against an independent host run. Start with systems and kernel access and shared time. Device execution is experimental; use the pinned Mojo/MAX environment and a working supported accelerator.
data.account-for-transfers-and-completion#Acc:
By default, every device call uploads all readable columns and resources. The transfer path packs only matching ranges and scatters writable results back to their original host stores.
Access declarations determine transfer directions.
The upload arrows carry both readable columns; the return arrows carry only Position. Gaps outside a selection remain untouched. Resource views and capture values bind separately from these columns. Allocation capacity can persist between calls; skipping unchanged data uploads requires the separate copy-reuse option.
run returns after the launch, synchronization, and writable component, read-write resource, and mutable-capture copy-back finish. The next system sees those host values. Downloads use owned staging and publish after successful synchronization. A transfer or synchronization failure discards unpublished staged outputs and drains the queue; if completion remains unknown, the world rejects further execution. Host effects are not rolled back. An adapter finalizer can raise after publication; its published outputs remain.
data.define-a-transferable-movement-stage#Def:
This stage keeps the particle names and uses Float32 arithmetic, including on host, so its arithmetic also compiles for Apple GPUs.
@fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable, TrivialRegisterPassable): """Particle coordinates, using device-compatible scalar arithmetic.""" var x: Float32 var y: Float32 @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable, TrivialRegisterPassable): """Particle displacement per unit of simulated time.""" var dx: Float32 var dy: Float32 @fieldwise_init struct Time(Copyable, Movable): """Shared simulated step length.""" var delta: Float32 Position and Velocity declare TrivialRegisterPassable, the component transfer requirement. Time is an ordinary resource: its recursively checked, pointer-free representation qualifies without that trait. A component trait check does not establish resource eligibility, and a host pointer field does not become a device allocation through byte copying.
Declare the readable inputs and writable position before selecting a target.

Args: context: Matching rows and read-only time. """ ref time = context.resources.get[Time]() for particle in context: ref position = particle.get[Position]() ref velocity = particle.get[Velocity]() position.x += velocity.dx * time.delta position.y += velocity.dy * time.delta move reads Velocity and Time and updates Position. The filter controls component matching and access; Resources separately declares resource access. include uploads and downloads the component, read uploads only, and write downloads only. A write-only component supports set, not get; initialize it for every visited row because its previous host bytes are not uploaded.
data.execute-and-compare-independent-runs#Exe:
The checked driver seeds 37 movers and an unmatched marker, runs two steps per target, and checks every coordinate before comparing sums.
def run_stage[backend: ExecutionBackend]() raises -> Position: """Runs two steps and checks both coordinates and an unmatched marker. Parameters: backend: Explicit target for this independent simulation. Raises: Error: If setup, execution, or a position check fails. Returns: The sum of the moving particles' final coordinates. """ var world = World[Position, Velocity]() world.resources.add(Time(0.25)) _ = world.storage.add_entities(Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 2), count=37) var marker = world.storage.add_entity(Position(-3, -3)) var scheduler = Scheduler[Position, Velocity](world^) scheduler.add_system(Move[backend]()) scheduler.run(steps=2) var total = Position(0, 0) for particle in scheduler.world.storage.query[move_filter](): ref position = particle.get[Position]() assert_almost_equal(position.x, 0.5) assert_almost_equal(position.y, 1.0) total.x += position.x total.y += position.y assert_equal(scheduler.world.storage.read[Position](marker).x, -3) return total def main() raises: """Reports device execution separately from a hardware skip. Raises: Error: If host checks, device execution, or parity checks fail. """ var host = run_stage[ExecutionBackend.HOST]() assert_almost_equal(host.x, 18.5) assert_almost_equal(host.y, 37.0) print("PASS: host particle checks") comptime if has_accelerator(): var device = run_stage[ExecutionBackend.DEVICE]() assert_almost_equal(device.x, host.x) assert_almost_equal(device.y, host.y) print("PASS: actual device execution and host/device parity") else: # A skip is an application choice; DEVICE itself never falls back. var empty = World[Position, Velocity]() empty.resources.add(Time(0.25)) var context = SystemContext(empty) with assert_raises(): context.run[move, backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE]() print("SKIP: device parity (no accelerator compilation support)") Each mover ends at (0.5, 1.0) and the marker stays at (-3, -3). The non-block multiple exercises device iteration beyond a trivial single-row launch. has_accelerator() gates this program’s optional validation; it is not a Larecs fallback. Once the program attempts DEVICE, initialization or execution errors propagate. The no-support branch instead checks that even an empty DEVICE request raises.

data.select-the-target-in-the-system#Select t:
The system specializes SystemContext.run for a ExecutionBackend value.
@fieldwise_init struct Move[backend: ExecutionBackend](System): """Selects the execution target explicitly.""" def update(mut self, mut context: SystemContext[...]) raises: """Runs one synchronous movement step. Args: context: Access to this simulation's world. Raises: Error: If resource preparation or execution fails. """ context.run[move, backend=Self.backend]() Move[ExecutionBackend.HOST]() uses sequential host execution, also the default when backend is omitted. Move[ExecutionBackend.DEVICE]() requests a device. The choice is compile-time; a runtime choice needs an explicit branch calling each specialization. The same choice is available on EntitySelection.run for exact selected ranges.
The execution mapping changes how often code outside the entity loop runs.
One row loop, three invocation mappings.
Store A and Store B are physical stores, which can belong to the same logical archetype. Sequential host calls cover stores or exact selected ranges; threaded calls may split those ranges. Device threads divide the packed rows in one launch using grid-stride iteration. Each matched row is visited once; row indices are local to the prepared context, never stable entity IDs.
data.troubleshooting-and-limits#Troubleshooti:
Failure or restriction Response DEVICE unavailable DEVICE raises even with no matching rows. Fix the accelerator/toolchain or explicitly choose HOST. There is no automatic fallback. Empty match on a working device Required resources and adapters still validate; no device allocation, upload, or launch occurs. Captures stay unchanged. Mutable adapters still prepare/finalize host output. Component transfer rejection Use components satisfying the device transfer check; keep owning collections on the host. Only accessed component types are checked. Ordinary resource rejection Use recursively pointer-free trivial values, or an adapter for an owner. PlainValue is a trusted declaration for opaque pointer-free trivial fields, not permission to transfer pointers. Resource access rejection Ordinary device resources allow read and read_write, not write. Mutable shared values require race-free writes. Closure or threaded/device combination rejected Device entry points are thin kernels. Lexical callables require sequential HOST; threaded=True requires HOST. Missing resource, including on an empty match Add every declared source during setup. Device availability is checked before resource preparation. Keep expensive work per particle; transfers and preparation can dominate a small kernel. Measure complete simulation steps before choosing a backend.

data: Read an owning sample collection through the same particle kernel on host and device. Start with shared resources and device selection. Adapter-backed device execution and mutable adapters follow the experimental status. This stage uses read-only views; kernel outputs remain per-entity components.
data.implement-validation-and-target-preparat:
The stateless ResourceAdapter checks the current owner and prepares the same descriptor type for each target.
struct GridAdapter(ResourceAdapter): """Prepares the same immutable descriptor for either target.""" comptime Source = Grid comptime View[mut: Bool] = GridView @staticmethod def validate(source: Self.Source) raises: """Validates shape and bounds before either target is prepared. Args: source: Current host owner. Raises: Error: If shape arithmetic overflows or sample counts disagree. """ if source.width <= 0 or source.height <= 0: raise Error("Grid dimensions must be positive") if source.width > Int(Int64.MAX) // source.height: raise Error("Grid dimensions overflow") if source.width * source.height != len(source.values): raise Error("Grid shape must match sample count") @staticmethod def bind_host(source: Self.Source) raises -> Self.View[False]: """Borrows the validated owner's samples without copying. Args: source: Owner retained through invocation completion. Returns: Host-local immutable descriptor. """ return { Pointer[Float32, ImmUntrackedOrigin]( unsafe_from_address=Int(source.values.unsafe_ptr()) ), source.width, source.height, } @staticmethod def prepare_device( source: Self.Source, mut cache: ResourceDeviceCache ) raises -> Self.View[False]: """Uploads samples through invocation-owned staging. Args: source: Current validated owner. cache: Source-type and device-context local allocations. Raises: Error: If allocation or upload fails. Returns: Descriptor containing a device-local sample pointer. """ return { cache.upload[Float32](0, Span(source.values)), source.width, source.height, } validate rejects zero dimensions, overflow, and inconsistent counts before binding either target, including empty entity matches. bind_host points into the retained source, never a temporary list. Its untracked origin makes the owner/lifetime obligations explicit; it does not transfer ownership.
prepare_device uses ResourceDeviceCache slot 0 for samples. cache.upload snapshots supported pointer-free trivial samples in owned staging before enqueueing. Larecs uploads the descriptor separately, using reserved slot -1. Give additional arrays distinct nonnegative stable slots; do not enqueue copies from external host pointers or temporary allocations. The cache belongs to the source type, world, and device context. It retains allocation capacity; by default preparation still uploads current data each run. Copy reuse can skip read-view preparation when revisions match.
data.keep-sources-and-views-valid-until-compl:
Larecs validates sources, leases them, and retains descriptors until synchronous completion, including the join of threaded host workers. Reentrant lookup, replacement, or removal of a bound source raises. Copying/moving/destroying leased storage through an escaped alias aborts. Neither a view, its pointers, nor references obtained from it may escape the invocation.
Every read view and all reachable storage must support concurrent reads without hidden mutation. Escaped aliases must not mutate, resize, relocate, or free the backing collection while a run uses it. An immutable pointer field alone does not establish that contract. Read adapters bind once on the coordinating host caller for threaded execution, then share the retained descriptor until join.
data.request-the-source-type-and-receive-its-:
Both Resources and the getter name the owning source type.
comptime move_filter = Filter().include[Position]().read[Velocity]() comptime move_resources = Resources().read[Time, Samples, Grid]() def move(context: KernelContext[move_filter, move_resources]): """Uses source-type lookup to read two portable views. Args: context: Particle rows, plain time, and adapted resources. """ ref samples = context.resources.get[Samples]() ref grid = context.resources.get[Grid]() ref time = context.resources.get[Time]() var scale = samples[0] + grid.last() for particle in context: ref position = particle.get[Position]() ref velocity = particle.get[Velocity]() position.x += velocity.dx * time.delta * scale position.y += velocity.dy * time.delta * scale Inside move, get[Samples]() returns ReadBuffer and get[Grid]() returns GridView, both immutable. Outside execution, world.resources.get[Grid]() returns the owning Grid. Lookup uses source identity, so two owners may share a view type without becoming the same resource. Adapters register automatically when the source is added or inserted with set; there is no adapter factory.
The driver adds both sources, changes the grid owner between runs, and checks validation without matching entities.
