data.separate-the-owner-from-the-kernel-view#:
The particle fields stay plain; time remains an ordinary read resource.
@fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable, TrivialRegisterPassable): """Particle coordinates, using device-compatible scalar arithmetic.""" var x: Float32 var y: Float32 @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable, TrivialRegisterPassable): """Particle displacement per unit of simulated time.""" var dx: Float32 var dy: Float32 @fieldwise_init struct Time(Copyable, Movable): """Shared simulated step length.""" var delta: Float32 These types have no heap ownership. The new resource sources below instead own collections and expose a different representation inside kernels.
Use BufferResource for a contiguous scalar buffer. Add a custom DevicePassableResource only when the kernel needs a domain-specific view, such as the last sample of a rectangular grid.
comptime Samples = BufferResource[DType.float32] @fieldwise_init struct Grid(DevicePassableResource): """Owns samples and dimensions on the host.""" comptime Adapter = GridAdapter var values: List[Float32] var width: Int var height: Int @fieldwise_init struct GridView(TrivialRegisterPassable): """Borrows immutable samples in the current target's address space.""" var values: Pointer[Float32, ImmUntrackedOrigin] var width: Int var height: Int def last(self) -> Float32: """Reads the final sample of a validated nonempty grid. Returns: The bottom-right sample. """ return self.values[unsafe_offset=self.width * self.height - 1] Samples owns its host collection and supplies the built-in immutable ReadBuffer with length and bounds-checked indexing. Do not index an empty buffer. Grid owns its List; GridView borrows samples through a pointer and exposes last(). Its dimensions must describe a nonempty grid. The pointer in a view is target-local: it refers to host memory during a host run and device memory during a device run.
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: Failure or restriction Fix Grid validation error Match dimensions and sample count before running. Empty entity matches do not bypass validation. Mutable declaration rejected Use explicit read for these sources, or implement the writer protocol and required capabilities. Ordinary device write-only resources remain unsupported. Invalid or stale view pointer Return target-local, owner/cache-backed memory; keep aliases from invalidating it. Do not byte-transfer a host pointer as an ordinary resource or capture. Unexpected stale samples with reuse enabled Reacquire the owner through get after each run, or explicitly invalidate after an escaped-reference write. Adapter finalizer raises Published outputs remain; the invocation is not a transaction. See device failure behavior. data.use-a-writer-view-only-when-the-adapter-:
This GridAdapter is read-only. Resources[Grid]() means read-write and is rejected; declare read explicitly. For shared output, first consider per-row results and a later reduction.
Current mutable adapters can opt into supports_mutation for sequential host writes and additionally supports_concurrent_mutation for threaded/device writes. These capabilities are author guarantees: an exclusive source lease does not prevent races among workers of one invocation. write selects fresh, adapter-initialized output; read_write preserves it. The descriptor remains immutable; its methods control backing writes. Preparation and finalization run once per invocation, even for empty matches, and mutable adapters prepare on every call despite copy reuse. The adapter reference and checked scatter example cover the hooks and atomic slot-reservation pattern.

data: Produce race-free shared results by writing per-particle output first and reducing it after run completes. Start with kernel access and read the execution restrictions before changing targets. Standalone synchronization primitives exist; automatic KernelContext.sync bindings and deferred retries do not.
data.match-ordering-and-backend-support#Match:
Public atomic operations default to relaxed ordering. Loads additionally accept acquire, stores release, and updates acquire, release, or acquire-release. Pass ordering at compile time. Relaxed counters do not publish adjacent ordinary data. Guards use acquire/release internally.
Target Available behavior CPU, NVIDIA, AMD Full initial scalar/guard operation set, with CPU-wide or whole-device scope. Backend compilation does not establish hardware correctness. Apple device Relaxed/acquire loads, relaxed/release stores, relaxed add/subtract. Strong CAS, ordered add/subtract, and guards are explicitly rejected. Device primitives need aligned, initialized device-accessible payload/state that stays alive until completion. Low-level unsafe view constructors do not allocate, transfer, or validate that memory. A canonical unlocked state must protect every overlapping guarded payload. Host/device allocations are separate domains; these primitives do not permit concurrent CPU/GPU access to one allocation.
Do not put an AtomicView or SyncView into an ordinary resource/capture and expect pointer transfer or automatic synchronization binding. Those raw-byte paths reject these views and aggregates containing them. Kernel binding adapters for these standalone owners remain unimplemented. A custom mutable resource adapter may implement a supported atomic protocol over its own target-local buffers; the checked scatter example demonstrates that separate contract.
data.run-and-troubleshoot#Run and troubleshoo:
The driver creates 37 movers, checks the reduction, and checks the standalone host operations.
def main() raises: """Checks particle reduction and standalone host primitives. Raises: Error: If setup, execution, or a check fails. """ var scheduler = Scheduler[Position, Velocity, Displacement]() scheduler.world.resources.add(Time(0.25)) _ = scheduler.world.storage.add_entities( Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 2), Displacement(0, 0), count=37 ) scheduler.add_system(Move()) scheduler.run(steps=1) check_primitives() print( "PASS: per-particle outputs, single-caller reduction, and host" " primitives" ) From the repository root, run pixi run mojo run -I src examples/particles/shared_outputs.mojo. Its PASS covers host reduction and primitives, not GPU synchronization. Use per-row or multi-pass output if a target lacks the operation you need; do not spin on Busy or invent a context.sync binding. Structural locks and resource leases protect invocation lifetimes and do not make shared writes race-free.

data.use-standalone-host-primitives-when-you-:
This independent check demonstrates atomic scalars and scoped guarded access outside ECS kernels.
def check_primitives() raises: """Checks target-local host primitives independently of ECS bindings. Raises: Error: If an atomic or guard check fails. """ var counter = AtomicValue[UInt32](0) var updates = counter.write_view() assert_equal(updates.fetch_add(1), UInt32(0)) var result = updates.compare_exchange(1, 5) assert_true(result.exchanged) assert_equal(result.observed, UInt32(1)) updates.store[Ordering.RELEASE](7) assert_equal(updates.load[Ordering.ACQUIRE](), UInt32(7)) var state = Synchronized[UInt32](10) var access = state.write_view() var attempt = access.try_read() assert_true(attempt.is_acquired()) var reader = attempt^.take() assert_equal(reader.value(), UInt32(10)) assert_false(access.try_write().is_acquired()) reader^.release() var write_attempt = access.try_write() assert_true(write_attempt.is_acquired()) var writer = write_attempt^.take() writer.value() += 5 writer^.release() var read_attempt = access.try_read() assert_true(read_attempt.is_acquired()) var after = read_attempt^.take() assert_equal(after.value(), UInt32(15)) AtomicValue owns a scalar; AtomicView borrows it. fetch_add returns the old value, and strong compare_exchange returns both success and the observed value. Only UInt32 and Int32 scalars are supported; add/subtract wrap at that width. Read views allow loads only.
Synchronized owns guarded data; SyncView borrows its canonical protection state. Multiple read guards may coexist, while a writer excludes all guards. try_read/try_write make at most one compare-exchange attempt. Test is_acquired before consuming the result with take. A false result means Busy, including a changed state or reader saturation. It is not an automatic wait or a successful skipped update.
References from guard.value() stay within the guard’s lifetime. Owners and guards are noncopyable; copied views share protection identity. Release by scope exit, including error unwinding, or by consuming guard^.release(). Errors do not roll back payload writes. There is no fairness, blocking wait, lock upgrade, or automatic retry: record required unfinished work for a later pass, or skip only if the application permits losing that update.

data: Run independent particle rows in concurrent host chunks, then compare their results with sequential execution. Start with systems and kernel access. Threading is experimental; it changes invocation boundaries within one kernel call, while systems still run in registration order.
data.configure-and-check-the-result#Configure:
This driver compares ordinary sequential execution, one-worker fallback, and a four-task configuration, each from a fresh world.
def run_stage[threaded: Bool](workers: Int) raises -> Position: """Checks parallel dispatch and whole-range fallback against exact values. Parameters: threaded: Whether to opt into the threaded engine. Args: workers: Submitted task budget; one exercises sequential fallback. Raises: Error: If configuration, execution, or a result check fails. Returns: Coordinate sums after two steps. """ var world = World[Position, Velocity]( execution_config=ThreadedExecutionConfig( workers=workers, chunks_per_worker=2, min_parallel_rows=0 ) ) world.resources.add(Time(0.25)) _ = world.storage.add_entities(Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 2), count=4097) var scheduler = Scheduler[Position, Velocity](world^) scheduler.add_system(Move[threaded]()) scheduler.run(steps=2) var total = Position(0, 0) for particle in scheduler.world.storage.query[move_filter](): ref position = particle.get[Position]() assert_almost_equal(position.x, 0.5) assert_almost_equal(position.y, 1.0) total.x += position.x total.y += position.y return total def main() raises: """Compares the sequential, one-worker, and multi-task call paths. Raises: Error: If an execution path disagrees. """ var sequential = run_stage[False](1) var fallback = run_stage[True](1) var threaded = run_stage[True](4) assert_equal(fallback.x, sequential.x) assert_equal(fallback.y, sequential.y) assert_equal(threaded.x, sequential.x) assert_equal(threaded.y, sequential.y) print( "PASS: sequential, one-worker fallback, and four-task particle parity" ) ThreadedExecutionConfig sets a submitted-task budget, not reserved cores or guaranteed OS thread overlap. min_parallel_rows=0 disables the size cutoff so the four-task case takes the chunk-dispatch path. All 4097 rows must end at (0.5, 1.0); the uneven count also exercises final short chunks. This result check alone does not prove simultaneous worker overlap.
From the repository root, run:
pixi run mojo run -I src examples/particles/threaded.mojo The PASS line confirms parity for all three call paths. Hardware concurrency claims need separate worker-overlap evidence, such as the repository’s threaded correctness tests.
data.respect-chunk-boundaries-and-lifetimes#R:
Parallel dispatch splits each physical store or selected range independently. Workers claim disjoint chunks dynamically; invocation order is unspecified. Code outside the row loop runs once per chunk. A row’s idx starts at zero in each host context, including each chunk: do not index a shared global output with it or treat it as an entity ID. KernelContext.thread_count remains one inside a host chunk. Cross-chunk dependencies need a later run after the join.
Default settings are one worker, four target chunks per worker, and a 65,536 matched-row cutoff. One worker or fewer rows than the cutoff preserves whole-range sequential calls, after all threaded eligibility checks. Empty matches invoke no kernel. Worker/chunk counts must be positive, their product representable, and the cutoff nonnegative.
Every explicitly threaded run acquires an extra structural lock, even for fallback and an already locked selection. Lock exhaustion raises before work starts. All fallible preparation precedes row writes, and all workers join before the call returns. Fatal worker/runtime failures offer no rollback.
Keep one coordinating caller for the world. Structural locks and resource leases are not mutexes for external aliases. Do not reenter execution, mutate backing resources, or resize/relocate storage through escaped aliases while workers run; copying, moving, replacing, or destroying an active world aborts. Avoid mutable globals and callees with hidden unsafe mutation.
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting:
Failure or restriction Fix Plain-value check fails Remove pointers/ownership from accessed components or ordinary read resources. PlainValue may declare opaque scalar-only StaticTuple/InlineArray fields; the author guarantees the entire representation is pointer-free and trivial. Mutable ordinary resource rejected Use explicit read, per-row component outputs, or an adapter declaring both mutation capabilities. A mutable adapter’s concurrent-write contract remains your responsibility. Small workload shows no improvement Measure dispatch overhead and complete steps; adjust the cutoff only after profiling. Structural lock exhaustion or locked world Release unrelated queries/selections before running or maintaining storage. Empty/exhausted cursors can still own locks. See the execution mapping, shared-write alternatives, and complete-step measurement.

Args: context: Matching rows and read-only time. """ ref time = context.resources.get[Time]() for particle in context: ref position = particle.get[Position]() ref velocity = particle.get[Velocity]() position.x += velocity.dx * time.delta position.y += velocity.dy * time.delta @fieldwise_init struct Move[threaded: Bool](System): """Opts into host chunks for this movement kernel.""" def update(mut self, mut context: SystemContext[...]) raises: """Moves disjoint rows and joins before returning. Args: context: Access to the simulation world. Raises: Error: If threaded eligibility or preparation fails. Parameters: threaded: Whether to opt into the threaded engine. Args: workers: Submitted task budget; one exercises sequential fallback. Raises: Error: If configuration, execution, or a result check fails. Returns: Coordinate sums after two steps. """ var world = World[Position, Velocity]( execution_config=ThreadedExecutionConfig( workers=workers, chunks_per_worker=2, min_parallel_rows=0 ) ) world.resources.add(Time(0.25)) _ = world.storage.add_entities(Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 2), count=4097) var scheduler = Scheduler[Position, Velocity](world^) scheduler.add_system(Move[threaded]()) scheduler.run(steps=2) var total = Position(0, 0) for particle in scheduler.world.storage.query[move_filter](): ref position = particle.get[Position]() assert_almost_equal(position.x, 0.5) assert_almost_equal(position.y, 1.0) total.x += position.x total.y += position.y return total def main() raises: """Compares the sequential, one-worker, and multi-task call paths. Raises: Error: If an execution path disagrees. """ var sequential = run_stage[False](1) var fallback = run_stage[True](1) var threaded = run_stage[True](4) assert_equal(fallback.x, sequential.x) assert_equal(fallback.y, sequential.y) assert_equal(threaded.x, sequential.x) assert_equal(threaded.y, sequential.y) print( "PASS: sequential, one-worker fallback, and four-task particle parity" ) View the source on GitHub

data:
Install the repository’s locked Pixi environment and run the first particle program. Then use Larecs from your own project, either as source or as a precompiled package.
Larecs runs on Linux x86-64 and macOS on Apple Silicon. Larecs 1.0.0b1 is a beta, so its APIs can still change. Pixi installs these dependencies:
Mojo >=1.0.0,<1.1.0 MAX >=26.5.0,<27 mojo-tracy >=1.1.0,<2 It resolves them from the channels conda-forge, https://repo.prefix.dev/max, and https://prefix.dev/tree-d (for mojo-tracy). pixi.lock pins the exact builds.
data.install-the-locked-environment#Install t:
Install Pixi, then run:
git clone https://github.com/larecs/larecs.git cd larecs pixi install --locked pixi run mojo --version pixi run mojo run -I src examples/particles/movement.mojo The program prints All particles reached their expected positions. and fails with an assertion error if a particle ends elsewhere. It runs on the host and needs no accelerator. To reproduce a result later, keep the checkout revision together with its pixi.lock.
Continue with Your first simulation, which explains this program.
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: Symptom Fix Import error for larecs Point -I at a directory that contains larecs/ source or larecs.mojoc. Compiler errors after a toolchain upgrade Restore the locked environment with pixi install --locked and rebuild the package. macOS linker error mentioning arm64e.x1 or libSystem.tbd Install an older macOS SDK. With SDKROOT unset, the repository’s activation script selects a compatible one. See the SDK workaround.
data.use-a-precompiled-package#Use a precompi:
Build the package with the toolchain your application uses. From the repository root:
mkdir -p /tmp/larecs-package pixi run mojo precompile src/larecs -o /tmp/larecs-package/larecs.mojoc pixi run mojo run -I /tmp/larecs-package examples/particles/movement.mojo Copy larecs.mojoc to your project’s include directory. Your application’s environment must provide compatible Mojo, MAX, and mojo-tracy builds from the channels above. Rebuild the package after you change the toolchain or the Larecs revision.
data.use-the-source-from-your-own-project#Use:
Run your program with the repository’s environment and pass the absolute path of src as an include directory. From the repository root:
larecs_root="$PWD" particle_project="$(mktemp -d)" cp examples/particles/movement.mojo "$particle_project/main.mojo" cd "$particle_project" pixi run --manifest-path "$larecs_root/pixi.toml" mojo run -I "$larecs_root/src" "$particle_project/main.mojo" This runs the same program from a directory outside the repository. For completion and diagnostics in your editor, add the same src path to the Mojo language server’s include directories.

data:
Measure and tune a simulation starts with checked particle results, then measures complete steps and profiles dominant systems. Use it after the core simulation, before choosing threading, device execution, copy reuse, or spatial maintenance cadence.
The existing benchmark methodology and reports retain scoped measurements and regression-check details. They remain evidence about their recorded workload, compiler, revision, and hardware.

Check equal simulation work first, then measure complete steps and profile the system that dominates them. Start with the first simulation. Optional targets must pass parity before timings influence your choice. A smaller kernel time alone does not establish a faster simulation.
data.capture-a-tracy-trace#Capture a Tracy tr:
Build a separate tracing binary inside Pixi’s environment so the linker sees the installed bindings and native library:
pixi run sh -c 'mojo build -I src -Xlinker -L"$CONDA_PREFIX/lib" -Xlinker -lmojotracy -DTRACY_ENABLED examples/particles/measurement.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-particles-tracy' pixi run tracy-profiler In Tracy, start discovery with Connect, then run /tmp/larecs-particles-tracy in another terminal. Inspect particles.complete_steps, particles.Move, and the internal zones for dominant work and repeated preparation. The twenty measured steps may be short; use a longer representative application run for profiling. Keep traced timings separate from optimized untraced comparison samples. pixi run profiling traces the repository’s benchmark suite instead of this particle driver.
data.establish-a-checked-workload#Establish a:
The measurement stage uses plain particle values and fixed time.
@fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable, TrivialRegisterPassable): """Particle coordinates, using device-compatible scalar arithmetic.""" var x: Float32 var y: Float32 @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable, TrivialRegisterPassable): """Particle displacement per unit of simulated time.""" var dx: Float32 var dy: Float32 @fieldwise_init struct Time(Copyable, Movable): """Shared simulated step length.""" var delta: Float32 Keeping the same fields, precision, entity count, and step length makes target comparisons meaningful. Validate every output needed by the application; a sum alone can hide compensating per-entity errors.
Use the unchanged movement loop as the measured work.
comptime move_filter = Filter().include[Position]().read[Velocity]() comptime move_resources = Resources().read[Time]() def move(context: KernelContext[move_filter, move_resources]): """Moves each row using its velocity and the shared step length. Args: context: Matching rows and read-only time. """ ref time = context.resources.get[Time]() for particle in context: ref position = particle.get[Position]() ref velocity = particle.get[Velocity]() position.x += velocity.dx * time.delta position.y += velocity.dy * time.delta Each step reads velocity and time and updates both position coordinates. Do not compare it with a variant that omits one coordinate, maintenance, or an output that the real application needs.
data.keep-results-with-their-conditions#Keep:
Link measurements with their workload, hardware, compiler, revision, method, uncertainty, and excluded costs. The host-dispatch investigation, partition comparison, and resource execution report provide scoped evidence. They do not predict the best target or layout on another machine.
Problem Next check Results differ Compare independent initial worlds, access declarations, write-only initialization and shared writes before timing. Disable copy reuse while diagnosing stale data. Device reports SKIP Record host coverage separately; a hardware skip is not device execution. Trace has no events Rebuild the final application with -DTRACY_ENABLED and the library flags, and connect the profiler before the run. Tiny or inconsistent timings Increase representative work, warm up, use repeated paired samples, and separate setup/output from the interval. Complete program: examples/particles/measurement.mojo """Measures complete host particle steps after checking their results.""" from std.testing import assert_almost_equal, assert_equal from larecs import ( ExecutionBackend, Filter, KernelContext, Resources, Scheduler, System, SystemContext, World, ) from std.time import perf_counter_ns from tracy import Zone @fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable, TrivialRegisterPassable): """Particle coordinates, using device-compatible scalar arithmetic.""" var x: Float32 var y: Float32 @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable, TrivialRegisterPassable): """Particle displacement per unit of simulated time.""" var dx: Float32 var dy: Float32 @fieldwise_init struct Time(Copyable, Movable): """Shared simulated step length.""" var delta: Float32 comptime move_filter = Filter().include[Position]().read[Velocity]() comptime move_resources = Resources().read[Time]() def move(context: KernelContext[move_filter, move_resources]): """Moves each row using its velocity and the shared step length. Args: context: Matching rows and read-only time. """ ref time = context.resources.get[Time]() for particle in context: ref position = particle.get[Position]() ref velocity = particle.get[Velocity]() position.x += velocity.dx * time.delta position.y += velocity.dy * time.delta @fieldwise_init struct Move(System): """Provides a named application zone around the movement invocation.""" def update(mut self, mut context: SystemContext[...]) raises: """Runs one synchronous kernel inside a Tracy zone. Args: context: Access to the simulation world. Raises: Error: If resource preparation or execution fails. """ with Zone("particles.Move"): context.run[move]() def main() raises: """Warms the simulation, times complete updates, and checks equal work. Raises: Error: If setup, stepping, or the final correctness check fails. """ var scheduler = Scheduler[Position, Velocity]() scheduler.world.resources.add(Time(0.25)) _ = scheduler.world.storage.add_entities( Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 2), count=4097 ) scheduler.add_system(Move()) scheduler.initialize() scheduler.update(steps=5) # warmup is outside the measured interval var start = perf_counter_ns() with Zone("particles.complete_steps"): scheduler.update(steps=20) var elapsed = perf_counter_ns() - start scheduler.finalize() # Validation and output are outside the timer. var count = 0 for particle in scheduler.world.storage.query[move_filter](): assert_almost_equal(particle.get[Position]().x, 6.25) assert_almost_equal(particle.get[Position]().y, 12.5) count += 1 assert_equal(count, 4097) print("PASS: 4097 particles after 25 steps") print("Measured 20 complete host steps (ns):", elapsed) View the source on GitHub
data.measure-complete-updates-separately-from:
The driver warms five steps, times twenty complete scheduler updates, and validates all 4097 particle results outside the interval.
def main() raises: """Warms the simulation, times complete updates, and checks equal work. Raises: Error: If setup, stepping, or the final correctness check fails. """ var scheduler = Scheduler[Position, Velocity]() scheduler.world.resources.add(Time(0.25)) _ = scheduler.world.storage.add_entities( Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 2), count=4097 ) scheduler.add_system(Move()) scheduler.initialize() scheduler.update(steps=5) # warmup is outside the measured interval var start = perf_counter_ns() with Zone("particles.complete_steps"): scheduler.update(steps=20) var elapsed = perf_counter_ns() - start scheduler.finalize() # Validation and output are outside the timer. var count = 0 for particle in scheduler.world.storage.query[move_filter](): assert_almost_equal(particle.get[Position]().x, 6.25) assert_almost_equal(particle.get[Position]().y, 12.5) count += 1 assert_equal(count, 4097) print("PASS: 4097 particles after 25 steps") print("Measured 20 complete host steps (ns):", elapsed) The interval includes system dispatch and synchronous run costs. It excludes compilation, world creation, initialization, warmup, finalization, validation, and printing. Each particle must finish at (6.25, 12.5) after all 25 steps. This small driver teaches timing boundaries; its single elapsed sample is not a performance claim or a backend benchmark.
From the repository root, build once and run the binary for repeated samples:
pixi run mojo build -I src examples/particles/measurement.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-particles /tmp/larecs-particles The program prints a correctness PASS and a machine-local elapsed nanosecond count. Record compilation separately. For a comparison, keep compiler version, optimization flags, hardware, workload, and revision fixed, warm each variant, alternate their order, and collect repeated paired samples without competing jobs. Use optimized builds without tracing, debug info, or sanitizers for timing. Follow the benchmark methodology for uncertainty, retained evidence, and regression checks.
data.profile-the-dominant-system#Profile the:
The system adds an application-level Tracy zone around its complete run call.
@fieldwise_init struct Move(System): """Provides a named application zone around the movement invocation.""" def update(mut self, mut context: SystemContext[...]) raises: """Runs one synchronous kernel inside a Tracy zone. Args: context: Access to the simulation world. Raises: Error: If resource preparation or execution fails. """ with Zone("particles.Move"): context.run[move]() particles.Move includes binding and execution, not only row arithmetic. Larecs also instruments internal work through Tracy. Compare system totals and call counts before changing a loop; time saved in a minor system has limited effect on a complete step. A host submission zone does not measure device kernel time in isolation; use a backend profiler for device activity and transfer details.
data.respect-explicit-simd-limits#Respect exp: Columns store one component struct per row: Position.x/y are fields in a Position column, not separate scalar columns. The public systems API exposes row iteration and no explicit CPU SIMD-batch interface. SIMD fields and compiler optimization do not create such an interface. Keep kernels on KernelContext rather than reaching into archetype storage to force a batch layout. Profile generated work before attributing a result to vectorization.
data.separate-arithmetic-from-boundary-costs#: Measurement boundary Include when comparing complete steps Sequential host Scheduler/system work, resource binding, store traversal, row processing, and required output handling. Threaded host The same work plus job preparation/dispatch/join; measure fallback and useful row-count thresholds. Device Packing, allocations when needed, input uploads, kernel launch/work, synchronization, downloads, and host scatter/publication. Copy reuse Validation and revisions, uploads that remain stale, mandatory output download, and invalidation caused by host edits or changing pack offsets. Spatial locality Input writes/dirty tracking, classification, sorting or partition transfer, location repair, and the passes that use the layout. Measure isolated kernels or maintenance passes to locate costs, then confirm the full-step result. A device can save arithmetic time while losing to transfers; a partitioned layout can improve one pass while increasing scan/binding costs. Keep maintenance inside the timed step when the real application requires it. Do not amortize a refresh across more steps than the correctness policy permits. After every change, rerun output checks and compare complete-step samples.

data: Iterating over entities can be done via classic for loops applied to queries. Queries provide read-only access to their results. In application logic, systems are the principal place for mutations; use a kernel to update components across all entities matching a filter.
data.iterating-over-queries#Iterating over qu:
As we have seen, we can iterate over queries using a for loop. Here, the control variable (“entity”) is an ArchetypeRowAccessor object, i.e., not technically an Entity, which is merely an identifier of an entity. Instead, the ArchetypeRowAccessor directly provides methods to get and check the existence of components, so that we do not need to call the storage’s methods for this, making the code more efficient. Since query’s iterator gives read-only access, components can only be read this way, not written. Use a kernel from a system to mutate matching components.
Because a query’s filter guarantees which components every matching entity has, get checks its component type against that filter at compile time: requesting a component the filter didn’t include is a compile error, not a runtime one. For a component the filter doesn’t guarantee – typically one you only conditionally access after checking has – use unsafe_get instead, which checks at runtime and raises if the component is missing.
for entity in world.storage.query[Filter().include[Position]()](): ref pos = entity.get[Position]() print( "Entity at position: (" + String(pos.x) + ", " + String(pos.y) + ")" ) if entity.has[Velocity](): # `Velocity` isn't included by this query's filter, so it isn't # guaranteed to exist on every matching entity -- `get` would be # a compile error here. `unsafe_get` is the checked-at-runtime # escape hatch for exactly this case. ref vel = entity.unsafe_get[Velocity]() # Also print the velocity print( " - with velocity (" + String(vel.dx) + ", " + String(vel.dy) + ")" ) Note
The ArchetypeRowAccessor is a temporary object that is created for each iteration. Therefore, it should not be stored in a container. Use ArchetypeRowAccessor.get_entity instead if you need to store the entity for later use.
data.processing-components-with-kernels#Proce:
A kernel is a component-processing function passed to SystemContext.run or EntitySelection.run. It receives a KernelContext and iterates over the entities matching its filter. The filter declares which components the kernel can write and which it can only read. The same kernel can run on the host or, for supported component types, an accelerator device.
The move_entities kernel declared above writes Position and only reads Velocity. The following direct construction demonstrates how the context invokes it:
var context = SystemContext(world) context.run[move_entities]() Calling the same kernel through a selection intersects the kernel filter with the selection’s saved ranges. The selection remains reusable; execution does not change its membership. Host row indices are local to each selected range, while device rows index the packed launch, so neither is a stable entity or selection-wide index.
In an application, the scheduler supplies this context to each system’s lifecycle methods, and the system calls run from there. The system is the scheduled unit of application logic; the kernel is the function it delegates filtered component processing to. See Systems and the scheduler for the complete pattern.
With partitioned spatial storage, ordinary queries traverse all matching blocks and staging rows. Logical archetype composition and query membership stay the same; row indices name a physical store and are not stable identifiers. Query locks and independent copy cursors apply across block boundaries too.
Queries return iteration.LockedEntityRange through HostStorage.Iterator. They share immutable store indices across copies; each copy owns its traversal position and a separate structural lock. Query access stays read-only. For execution on changed rows, use SystemContext batch operations and EntitySelection.run; low-level storage ranges are described in batch creation.
data.queries#Queries:
The query method of HostStorage allows to iterate over all entities with or without a specific set of components. It takes a compile-time Filter specifying the components that each entity we look for must have (and, optionally, must not have). For example, if we want to iterate over all entities with a Position and a Velocity component, we can do this as follows:
from larecs import World, Filter, SystemContext, KernelContext @fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): var x: Float64 var y: Float64 @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable): var dx: Float64 var dy: Float64 comptime move_filter = Filter().include[Position].read[Velocity]() def move_entities(context: KernelContext[move_filter]): for entity in context: ref pos = entity.get[Position]() ref vel = entity.get[Velocity]() pos.x += vel.dx pos.y += vel.dy def main() raises: var world = World[Position, Velocity]() # Add entities with different components _ = world.storage.add_entity() _ = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0)) _ = world.storage.add_entity(Velocity(1, 0)) _ = world.storage.add_entity(Position(1, 0), Velocity(1, 0)) # Query all entities that have a position. var query = world.storage.query[Filter().include[Position]()]() # Of the entities we have just added, # two have a position component print(len(query)) # "2" # Query iterators are copyable. A copy starts at the same position. var query_copy = query.copy() # Now let us iterate over the queried entities # (`^` transfers this iterator into the loop without copying it). for entity in query^: ref pos = entity.get[Position]() print( "Entity at position: (" + String(pos.x) + ", " + String(pos.y) + ")" ) # The copy has an independent cursor, so it can be consumed separately. for _ in query_copy^: pass The filter can also exclude entities that have certain components. For example, if we want to iterate over all entities that have a Position component but not a Velocity component, we can do this using exclude:
var excluding_query = world.storage.query[ Filter().include[Position].exclude[Velocity]() ]() print(len(excluding_query)) # "1" Furthermore, we can also query for entities that have exactly the components we are looking for but no more. This can be done using exclusive. For example, if we want to iterate over all entities that have only a Position component, we can do this as follows:
var exclusive_query = world.storage.query[ Filter().include[Position].exclusive() ]() print(len(exclusive_query)) # "1" Note
Determining the length of a query is not a trivial operation and may require an internal iteration if the ECS involves many components. Therefore, it is advisable to avoid applying the len function to queries in “hot” code. Nonetheless, the len function is much faster than counting entities manually by iterating over a query.

data:
Not all data in a world is associated with
specific entities. This often applies to
parameters (such as a time step),
global state variables (such as the current time),
or spatial data structures (such as a grid displaying
entity positions). These data are called resources.
data.adding-and-accessing-resources#Adding an:
The examples below access a World directly to introduce the resource API. During application execution, resource changes should generally be owned by a system, keeping them in the same scheduled lifecycle as entity and component changes. Its lifecycle methods can access resources through context.world[].resources.
Resources can be accessed and added via the resources field of World. Adding a resource is done via the resources.add method:
def main() raises: var world = World[Position, Velocity]() # Add the `Time` resource world.resources.add(Time(0.0)) The resources attribute also allows us to access and change resources via get and set. Unlike their component-related counterparts, these operations need no entity argument: a resource is selected only by its type.
ResourceStorage.get intentionally returns a reference with UnsafeAnyOrigin, preserving the mutability of the storage access. It should keep this origin until Mojo’s origin system can model the ownership relation between the resource container and its separately allocated resource values. Tying the returned reference to the storage origin is not a suitable interim replacement.
# Change a resource value via a reference world.resources.get[Time]().delta = 1.0 # Get a reference to a resource ref time = world.resources.get[Time]() # Change the resource value via the reference time.delta = 2.0 # Replace the entire resource through the returned reference world.resources.get[Time]() = Time(3.0) assert_equal(world.resources.get[Time]().delta, 3.0) The add and set methods can add or set multiple resources at once. For example, consider the additional resources Temperature and SelectedEntities, each defined just like Time above.
We can add and set them as follows:
# Add multiple resources world.resources.add( Temperature(20.0), SelectedEntities(List[Entity]()) ) # Set multiple resources world.resources.set( Temperature(30.0), Time(2.0) ) These operations are strict by default:
add raises if a requested resource type already exists. get and remove raise if the requested resource does not exist. set raises if any requested resource does not exist and does not update any of them. Use set[add_if_not_found=True](...) when missing resources should be inserted. For example, set can explicitly recreate a missing resource:
world.resources.remove[Temperature]() world.resources.set[add_if_not_found=True](Temperature(25.0)) assert_equal(world.resources.get[Temperature]().temperature, 25.0) Like components, resources can own heap memory, as SelectedEntities does with its List. A world holds at most one value per resource type, so a resource suits data of any size that the whole simulation shares. Owning resources work in sequential host kernels; threaded and device kernels need a pointer-free value or an adapter, as described in Using resources in kernels.
# Create entities and add them to the selected entities for i in range(10): var entity = world.storage.add_entity(Position(Float64(i), Float64(i))) world.resources.get[SelectedEntities]().entities.append(entity)
data.defining-resources#Defining resources:
Similar to components, resources are defined via structs. That is, each resource has a specific type, and having two resources of the same type is not possible.
However, in contrast to components, the (potentially) used resources do not need to be known at compile time but can be dynamically added to the world and are keyed by their runtime type name.
from larecs import ( ExecutionBackend, World, Entity, SystemContext, KernelContext, Filter, Resources, ResourceType, ) from std.testing import assert_equal, assert_false, assert_true @fieldwise_init struct Time(ResourceType, TrivialRegisterPassable): var delta: Float64 @fieldwise_init struct Temperature(ResourceType): var temperature: Float64 @fieldwise_init struct SelectedEntities(ResourceType): var entities: List[Entity] @fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): var x: Float64 var y: Float64 @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable): var dx: Float64 var dy: Float64 A resource must conform to ResourceType (Copyable & Deinitable). SelectedEntities owns a List, which sequential host kernels accept. Device and threaded kernels check a resource’s representation rather than a declared trait: Time and Temperature both qualify because they hold only a Float64. Time additionally declares TrivialRegisterPassable, which these checks do not require.
data.invocation-lifetime-and-failures#Invocat:
run completes synchronously. Larecs retains sources and descriptors throughout execution, rejects reentrant lookup/replacement/removal of bound sources, and rejects duplicate source declarations. Previously escaped UnsafeAnyOrigin references must not mutate or resize the source while a kernel uses its view; views and references must not escape the invocation. Copying or destroying leased storage through an escaped alias aborts because lifecycle operations cannot raise.
Device component, capture, and resource downloads use owned staging and publish only after synchronization succeeds. On failure Larecs drains the queue and propagates the error; if completion remains unknown, further execution on the world raises. Failed calls discard staged outputs, without promising rollback of other host effects. Empty device matches still validate resources and adapters but perform no device allocation, upload, or launch.
data.mutable-adapted-resources-experimental#M:
An adapter can also give kernels a writer view, so shared output such as a per-cell grid is filled without a MutCapture and with the same kernel on every target. The access declaration selects the view:
Declaration get[T]() returns Output before the kernel runs Resources().read[T]() T.View[False] Not applicable Resources().write[T]() T.View[True] Fresh, initialized by the adapter Resources().read_write[T]() T.View[True] Existing contents preserved Read and writer views can be different types:
struct GridAdapter(ResourceAdapter): comptime Source = Grid comptime View[mutable: Bool] = GridFill if mutable else GridRead comptime supports_mutation = True comptime supports_concurrent_mutation = True Both capabilities default to False. supports_mutation admits write and read_write declarations for sequential host runs. Device and threaded=True runs also require supports_concurrent_mutation. Declare it only if every writer-view operation is safe under concurrent use, for example because slots are reserved with atomics and then written disjointly. Larecs leases the source exclusively for the invocation. This does not prevent races between the GPU threads or host workers of one kernel: you are responsible for safe resource access. Unsupported combinations fail compilation.
The descriptor a kernel receives is immutable. A writer view holds pointers to adapter-managed backing buffers, such as slots, per-cell counters, reductions, and error flags, and mutates them through its own methods. Mutable adapters implement four hooks that receive the full ResourceAccess mode, so write can initialize fresh output while read_write preserves it:
Hook When Larecs calls it bind_host_mutable[access](mut source) Once before host kernels run. On the host, kernels write the source’s buffers directly. Also called for device runs without matching rows. prepare_device_mutable[access](mut source, mut cache) Once before a device launch. Use cache.fill for fresh output and cache.upload_mutable to preserve contents. stage_device_results[access](mut source, mut cache) After the launch is queued. Stage every output with cache.download. finalize[access](mut source) Once after all kernel work completed and device outputs were published. Use it to clamp counters or report overflow. Preparation and finalization run once per invocation, across every matching archetype, selected range, threaded chunk, and device launch, including runs with no matching rows. Output is never reset per archetype or worker. Device runs use the world’s device queue and cache; buffers and staging stay alive until completion. Mutable adapted sources are prepared on every run, even in worlds that reuse device copies. Size host targets before staging downloads; they are written only after the queue completes.
Failures follow the invocation rules:
Host writes are not rolled back. If preparation fails after write initialization, the source stays initialized, and finalize does not run. Device outputs are published only after synchronization succeeds. A failed run discards them. If finalize raises, the run raises, but published outputs remain and the world stays usable. examples/scatter_resource.mojo is a complete example. Writers reserve per-cell slots with atomic counters and count dropped writes; finalize clamps the counters. The same thin kernel runs sequentially, threaded, and on a device. Run it with pixi run scatter-example. Slot order within a cell depends on scheduling.
Migrating existing adapters Adapters written for the read-only API need three changes:
Replace comptime View = MyView with comptime View[mut: Bool] = MyView. Change bind_host and prepare_device to return Self.View[False]. Remove comptime KernelView = MyView from the source. KernelView still exists as an alias for View[False]. Adapters that do not opt into mutation keep their behavior. Mutable declarations of them now fail with “mutable access requires Adapter.supports_mutation”.
data.portable-owning-resources#Portable ownin:
Use BufferResource for a contiguous scalar collection. The same kernel requests the original source type and receives its read-only ReadBuffer view on both backends:
from larecs import ExecutionBackend, BufferResource, Filter, KernelContext, Resources, SystemContext, World comptime Samples = BufferResource[DType.int32] comptime required = Resources().read[Samples]() def add_sample(context: KernelContext[Filter().include[Int32](), required]): ref samples = context.resources.get[Samples]() for entity in context: entity.get[Int32]() += samples[0] def main() raises: var world = World[Int32]() world.resources.add(Samples([Int32(7), Int32(8)])) _ = world.storage.add_entities(Int32(1), count=37) var context = SystemContext(world) context.run[add_sample]() context.run[add_sample, backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE]() world.resources.get[Samples]().samples[0] = 9 context.run[add_sample]() Device execution requires a working accelerator. By default, the samples are uploaded on every device run; worlds that reuse unchanged device copies skip the upload while the source is unchanged. Device allocation capacity is reused. The host source remains unchanged by device view access. ReadBuffer has len and bounds-checked indexing; empty buffers have length zero and must not be indexed.
Defining a custom portable resource Implement DevicePassableResource when your resource owns data that cannot be copied directly to a device, or needs a domain-specific kernel API. Keep the owning host type, its kernel view, and transfer logic separate:
Type Contains Used by Grid Owning List and current dimensions Application code between runs GridView Immutable sample pointer, dimensions, and sampling methods The same kernel on either backend GridAdapter Static validation and view preparation methods Larecs during run The source declares its Adapter as a compile-time member. The adapter declares the matching Source and a View[mut: Bool] mapping; it needs no constructor or instance fields. A read-only adapter maps both access kinds to one view type. The source’s View and KernelView (an alias for View[False]) default to the adapter’s mapping. Every method reads the current source, including configuration such as dimensions.
This complete example uses a rectangular grid. Its view exposes last() to keep pointer arithmetic inside the resource API. A scientific view can instead provide interpolation, coordinate lookup, or other read-only operations.
from std.sys import has_accelerator from std.testing import assert_equal from larecs import ( ExecutionBackend, DevicePassableResource, ResourceAdapter, ResourceDeviceCache, Filter, KernelContext, Resources, SystemContext, World, ) @fieldwise_init struct Grid(DevicePassableResource): """Owns current host samples and grid metadata.""" comptime Adapter = GridAdapter var values: List[Int32] var width: Int var height: Int @fieldwise_init struct GridView(TrivialRegisterPassable): """Portable read-only descriptor over current target-local samples.""" var values: Pointer[Int32, ImmUntrackedOrigin] var width: Int var height: Int def last(self) -> Int32: """Reads the last sample of this validated nonempty grid. Returns: Last grid sample. """ return self.values[unsafe_offset=self.width * self.height - 1] struct GridAdapter(ResourceAdapter): """Stateless adapter using current dimensions and cached sample capacity.""" comptime Source = Grid comptime View[mut: Bool] = GridView @staticmethod def validate(source: Self.Source) raises: """Checks a nonempty rectangular grid before preparing either target. Args: source: Current host owner. Raises: Error: If dimensions overflow or do not match sample storage. """ if source.width <= 0 or source.height <= 0: raise Error("This grid requires positive dimensions") if source.width > 9223372036854775807 // source.height: raise Error("Grid dimensions overflow") if source.width * source.height != len(source.values): raise Error("Grid dimensions must match sample count") @staticmethod def bind_host(source: Self.Source) raises -> Self.View[False]: """Borrows immutable samples from the validated host owner. Args: source: Current validated source. Raises: Error: If descriptor preparation fails. Returns: Descriptor over host samples. """ return { Pointer[Int32, ImmUntrackedOrigin]( unsafe_from_address=Int(source.values.unsafe_ptr()) ), source.width, source.height, } @staticmethod def prepare_device( source: Self.Source, mut cache: ResourceDeviceCache ) raises -> Self.View[False]: """Uploads current samples and returns the same descriptor type. Args: source: Current validated source. cache: Source-type, context-local allocation cache. Raises: Error: If sample allocation or upload fails. Returns: Descriptor over device samples. """ return { cache.upload[Int32](0, Span(source.values)), source.width, source.height, } validate runs before preparation on either backend, even when no entities match. Check sample counts and arithmetic here; a trivial view descriptor does not prove that its pointer indexing is valid. This grid rejects empty storage, so last() is always defined after successful validation.
bind_host borrows the owner’s samples without copying. Its untracked immutable pointer relies on Larecs retaining the source throughout the invocation; it must never point into a temporary local collection. prepare_device uploads the samples through the supplied cache and returns the same descriptor with a device pointer. Larecs uploads the descriptor itself; the adapter does not need to.
Registering and using the custom resource Declare read access using the source type, and keep that same type in get[Grid](). Inside the kernel the result is an immutable GridView, on both host and device. Outside the kernel, world.resources.get[Grid]() returns the owning Grid for edits. The following continues the example above:
comptime required = Resources().read[Grid]() def add_grid_sample( context: KernelContext[Filter().include[Int32](), required] ): """Adds the grid's last sample to each matching component. Args: context: Component rows and the read-only GridView binding. """ ref grid = context.resources.get[Grid]() for entity in context: entity.get[Int32]() += grid.last() def main() raises: """Uses one custom resource and kernel on the host and, if available, device. Raises: Error: If resource validation, execution, or a result check fails. """ var world = World[Int32]() world.resources.add(Grid([Int32(1), Int32(2), Int32(3), Int32(9)], 2, 2)) var entity = world.storage.add_entity(Int32(1)) var context = SystemContext(world) context.run[add_grid_sample]() assert_equal(world.storage.get[Int32](entity), 10) # World-side access returns the owning Grid, so samples can be edited. world.resources.get[Grid]().values[3] = 5 context.run[add_grid_sample]() assert_equal(world.storage.get[Int32](entity), 15) comptime if has_accelerator(): context.run[add_grid_sample, backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE]() assert_equal(world.storage.get[Int32](entity), 20) assert_equal(world.resources.get[Grid]().values[3], 5) The host calls always run; the device call runs when an accelerator is available. No explicit binding registration or manual transfer is required. Editing the owner between runs changes what the next invocation sees. Kernel results go to components; the read-only resource is never downloaded or changed by the kernel. Host-only resources can continue implementing ResourceType without an adapter.
Adapter allocation and access rules Every adapter must support concurrent reads of its read view, View[False], on the view’s execution target. View methods and all reachable memory must permit concurrent reads without hidden unsafe mutation. No escaped alias may mutate, resize, relocate, or free backing data before invocation completion; immutable pointer fields alone do not establish this guarantee. This is a universal adapter contract, with no capability marker.
Threaded host calls accept adapted sources only through explicit read declarations. The caller validates and binds each source once, then shares the same descriptor and sample storage across jobs. Resource leases and descriptor owners remain alive until all workers join, including whole-range fallback. Ordinary pointer-free read resources also work without an adapter. Ordinary mutable resources remain unsupported by this engine; mutable adapted resources require concurrent mutation support.
Use nonnegative cache slots for sample allocations. Slot -1 is reserved for Larecs’s view descriptor. For multiple arrays, give each array its own stable slot, such as 0 for samples and 1 for coordinates. Each world keeps a separate cache per source type, tied to its device context. Capacity is reused, and every preparation uploads current contents. Adapters need no revision tracking of their own: in worlds that reuse device copies, Larecs skips prepare_device entirely while the source is unchanged.
The cache accepts supported pointer-free trivial sample values, snapshots them in native owned staging, and returns an immutable device pointer. Adapters must use cache-owned allocations and this upload helper; queued copies from external host pointers or pointers to temporary allocations violate the lifetime contract. Views may contain immutable pointers and trivial metadata; mutable pointer fields are rejected. Adapters remain responsible for valid device addresses and pointee interpretation.
There is no adapter factory or instance. Registration happens automatically on add and insert-on-set; source types identify bindings, so two resources may share the same view type. A wrapper can adapt a third-party owner. See the compiled grid example.
Adapters without mutation support accept only read, including on the host; Resources[AdaptedSource]() and mutable declarations fail compilation. get[Source]() always returns the associated view; kernels cannot access the owner. Edit the world-side owner between runs, including whole-instance assignment through world.resources.get[T]() = T(...); the next run validates and uploads the new source without rebinding. Copied worlds have independent host owners and empty resource caches.
data.removing-resources#Removing resources:
One or multiple resources can be removed via the remove method. The existence of a resource is checked via the has method.
When removing multiple types, removals happen in argument order. If a later type is missing, remove raises after any earlier types have already been removed. Check all types with has first when the operation must be all-or-nothing.
# Remove the `Time` and the `Temperature` resource world.resources.remove[Time, Temperature]() # Check if the `Time` resource exists assert_false(world.resources.has[Time]()) # `set[add_if_not_found=True]` can insert it again world.resources.set[add_if_not_found=True](Time(4.0)) assert_true(world.resources.has[Time]())
data.resource-permissions#Resource permission:
Resources[T]() preserves read_write access. Prefer explicit declarations:
comptime required = Resources().read[Time]().read_write[Statistics]() A read getter is immutable and its device buffer is never downloaded. read_write permits mutable get[T]() and copies device changes back after successful completion. Host write[T]() offers set[T](value) only; it rejects get[T](). Device write-only resources are unsupported because conditional shared writes could publish uninitialized data. Applications must synchronize concurrent writes to ordinary shared resources themselves.
data.reusing-unchanged-device-copies-experime:
By default every backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE run uploads all resources and readable component columns it declares, even if they did not change. Worlds that call world.reuse_device_copies(True) skip uploads of data that is unchanged since its device copy was made. For adapted resources this skips the whole prepare_device call; validation and leases still run on every call. Written data is still downloaded after every run.
Larecs cannot see what you do with a reference after it returns it. It tracks revisions that advance on every Larecs access that may mutate data:
Resources: add, set, get through a mutable world, host runs declaring write or read_write, and device runs writing the resource. Component columns, per type and physical store: world.storage.get and set, kernel runs writing the type, and every structural change, spatial reordering, or partition move of the store. Use world.resources.read[T]() and world.storage.read[T](entity) for reads between device runs: they return immutable references and keep device copies reusable, whereas get on a mutable world always counts as a mutation. Read queries never count as mutations.
Component columns are reused per contiguous store range. Kernels with different filters on the same component type pack stores at different offsets, so alternating them uploads that column again each time.
Re-obtain or invalidate. In a world that reuses device copies, never mutate a resource through a reference obtained before a later Larecs call or through a raw pointer without telling Larecs. Re-obtain the reference with get after each run, or call world.resources.invalidate_device[T]() (or world.invalidate_device_copies() for everything) after the mutation. Otherwise the next device run silently reads the stale device copy.
world.reuse_device_copies(True) # Reading through `read` keeps an unchanged device copy reusable. _ = world.resources.read[Time]().delta # A pointer kept across runs bypasses revision tracking... var time_ptr = Pointer(to=world.resources.get[Time]()) time_ptr[].delta = 4.0 # ...so invalidate after mutating through it. world.resources.invalidate_device[Time]() world.reuse_device_copies(False) A failed device run marks the copies it touched as unknown, so the next run uploads them again. Disabling reuse, removing a resource, and copying the world discard device copy records.
data.using-resources-in-kernels#Using resourc:
A kernel declares the resource types it may access with a compile-time Resources list. Pass that list as the second parameter of KernelContext, then retrieve a resource through context.resources.get[T]():
var mover = world.storage.add_entity( Position(0.0, 0.0), Velocity(2.0, 1.0) ) def move_with_time( context: KernelContext[ Filter().include[Position].read[Velocity](), Resources[Time](), ] ): ref time = context.resources.get[Time]() for entity in context: ref pos = entity.get[Position]() ref vel = entity.get[Velocity]() pos.x += vel.dx * time.delta pos.y += vel.dy * time.delta var context = SystemContext(world) context.run[move_with_time]() # `Time.delta` is 2.0, so the velocity moved the entity by (4.0, 2.0) ref position = world.storage.get[Position](mover) assert_equal(position.x, 4.0) assert_equal(position.y, 2.0) Here, Resources[Time]() makes Time available to move_with_time. get[Time]() returns a mutable reference, so a kernel may also update the resource. Such changes remain in the world’s resource storage after the kernel finishes. Every declared resource must already have been added to the world; otherwise SystemContext.run raises an error.
The direct SystemContext construction keeps this example focused on the resource API. In application logic, call run from a system lifecycle method, as shown in Systems and the scheduler.
A resource is one shared mutable value for every entity processed by the kernel. Concurrent reads need no special handling. Writes from GPU threads must be synchronized or otherwise made race-free; in particular, do not update a shared resource once per entity without an atomic or reduction strategy. Writing per-entity results to components and reducing them in a separate step is often simpler. Keep side effects inside the entity loop, because the number of kernel calls depends on the execution target:
Sequential host: one call per non-empty matching physical store. With spatial partitioning, one archetype can have several physical stores. EntitySelection.run calls the kernel once per selected row range instead. Threaded host: one call per kernel chunk; each store or selected range is split into chunks that may run concurrently. Device: one launch covers all matching rows. Host kernels may also capture surrounding values and access resources through context.run(kernel). See Capturing host kernels for an example. Device entry points use the non-capturing context.run[kernel]() form.
Import ExecutionBackend from larecs and replace the host run call with:
context.run[move_with_time, backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE]() Host execution is the default. DEVICE requires a working accelerator and raises when unavailable, including for empty matches; it never falls back to HOST.
For device execution, components must conform to TrivialRegisterPassable. Ordinary resources need a supported pointer-free representation with trivial copy, move, and destruction. Numeric values, Bool, and aggregates of those values are accepted without declaring TrivialRegisterPassable. Owning collections, host pointers, and opaque representations (including fixed Array fields in this increment) are rejected. Host kernels still support owning resources.

data.add-read-replace-and-remove-resources#Ad:
ResourceStorage manages the world’s resources:
Method Effect Raises when ResourceStorage.add Inserts values A type is already present ResourceStorage.get Returns a reference to the value The type is missing ResourceStorage.set Replaces existing values Any type is missing; then no value changes. With add_if_not_found=True, it inserts missing types instead. ResourceStorage.remove Removes values A type is missing Do not keep a resource reference across removal or replacement.
data.declare-kernel-access#Declare kernel acc:
comptime move_filter = Filter().include[Position]().read[Velocity]() comptime move_resources = Resources().read[Time]() def move(context: KernelContext[move_filter, move_resources]): """Advances every particle by its velocity times the step length. Args: context: The matching rows and the declared resources. """ ref time = context.resources.get[Time]() for particle in context: ref position = particle.get[Position]() ref velocity = particle.get[Velocity]() position.x += velocity.dx * time.delta position.y += velocity.dy * time.delta A kernel declares its resources with Resources, separately from its component filter:
Declaration Access through the kernel read[T]() Read with get read_write[T]() Read and write with get write[T]() Write with set only, on the host; device kernels reject it Resources[T]() Read and write, like read_write Every declared resource must exist in the world when you call SystemContext.run; otherwise run raises.
On the sequential host, a resource can own collections such as a List. Every kernel call in one run sees the same resource value. Because one run can call the kernel several times, change per-step values in a system’s update, as ConfigureTime does, rather than in the kernel.
data.define-a-resource#Define a resource: A resource is a struct that conforms to ResourceType, which requires Copyable and Deinitable. Copyable, Movable satisfies both. A world holds at most one value per resource type, and resource types do not appear in the world’s component list.
data.next-steps#Next steps: Use portable resources covers threaded and device restrictions and adapters for resources that own data.
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: Symptom Fix run raises because Time is missing Add Time with world.resources.add before you start the scheduler. Compile error on resource access Check the kernel’s Resources declaration; the component filter does not grant resource access.

data:
Spatial clustering groups equal-key entities together in memory within each component archetype. It is an opt-in locality optimization. It does not change entity IDs or query membership and does not provide exact neighbor queries.
Register one classifier with an explicit read-only filter, then call world.maintain_spatial() when your application wants to refresh row order. Configuration belongs to the classifier value; the world owns it and copies it when the world is copied. Registration does not classify or move any rows.
from larecs import World, Filter, SpatialClassifier, grid_cell, morton_key_3d from larecs.entity import EntityAccessor from std.testing import assert_equal @fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): var x: Float64 var y: Float64 comptime spatial_filter = Filter().read[Position]() @fieldwise_init struct Grid(SpatialClassifier): comptime Accessor = EntityAccessor[spatial_filter] var cell_size: Float64 def classify(self, entity: Self.Accessor) raises -> UInt64: """Computes a planar grid key from declared read-only inputs. Args: entity: Position accessor valid only during classification. Raises: Error: If the coordinates or configured cell size are invalid. Returns: The collision-free Morton key for the current cell. """ ref position = entity.get[Position]() return morton_key_3d( grid_cell(position.x, self.cell_size), grid_cell(position.y, self.cell_size), ) def main() raises: """Demonstrates explicit maintenance and stable entity identities. Raises: Error: If world setup, maintenance, or validation fails. """ var world = World[Position]() var a = world.storage.add_entity(Position(12, 0)) var b = world.storage.add_entity(Position(-1, 0)) world.register_spatial_classifier[spatial_filter](Grid(cell_size=4)) world.maintain_spatial() # Entity IDs still find the same component values after row movement. assert_equal(world.storage.get[Position](a).x, 12) assert_equal(world.storage.get[Position](b).x, -1) Filter.read permits immutable access. Writable include/write declarations are rejected at registration, as is an accessor type that does not match the registration filter. Inclusion, exclusion, and exclusive matching use the same rules as ordinary queries. Nonmatching archetypes are never classified or moved. The first implementation accepts one classifier per world; a second registration raises and leaves the existing policy in place.
The classifier must be deterministic for unchanged component inputs and policy configuration. It must not mutate the world or retain the accessor or component references. Equal UInt64 keys identify a cluster. In the default reordering mode, ascending numeric key order determines group order. Tie order is not guaranteed. Avoid arbitrary hashes when you need locality between clusters.
grid_cell uses floor, so -0.1 with cell size 1 maps to cell -1. Inputs must be finite and cell size must be positive. Each resulting cell must lie in [-1048576, 1048575]. morton_key_3d interleaves three biased signed 21-bit cells without collisions in that range; its default z=0 supports planar grids. Out-of-range coordinates raise rather than wrapping or merging cells. Use a custom UInt64 encoding if your application’s bounds differ.
Each explicit maintenance pass classifies distinct dirty eligible entities once using their final component values. Repeated writes deduplicate, and a clean pass returns without scanning rows. Registration and structural mutations (creation, deletion, add/remove/replace, and batch/selection changes) request a full rebuild. When every allocated ID is dirty, maintenance uses contiguous full classification. Only affected eligible archetypes have their cached keys checked and reordered; unchanged entities can still move to restore contiguous groups.
Mutable storage.get[T](entity) access marks classifier inputs even when used only to read. Prefer read-only queries for observation. Setters mark overlapping inputs; host kernels conservatively mark their matching declared writable ranges, including exact selected ranges. Read-only declarations and unrelated component writes do not invalidate classifier inputs. Device writable copy-back marks the same host identities; classification remains on the host.
Raw pointers and low-level archetype access bypass tracking. After such writes, call world.storage.mark_spatial_dirty(entity) for each affected live identity, or world.invalidate_spatial() (also available on storage) for a full rebuild. External changes to otherwise owned policy configuration require full invalidation. These calls only invalidate; they do not require an unlocked world or move rows. Do not retain component references across maintenance, including clean passes.
Maintenance prepares all keys (and reordering permutations in the default mode) before moving rows, so a classifier error leaves row order and committed keys unchanged, retains pending invalidations for retry, and preserves the original error message. Movement uses typed component lifecycle operations, including for heap-backed columns the classifier does not read. Fatal allocation or lifecycle failures do not provide rollback.
Maintenance requires an unlocked world. Release live queries and selections first, and do not keep component references across the call. In a system, use context.world[].maintain_spatial() after releasing its selections. Writes, entity changes, kernel completion, and system completion never invoke maintenance automatically. Device copy-back updates current host values; the next explicit pass classifies invalidated identities from those values, and subsequent host/device kernels see the new row order.
Choose a cadence by measuring your workload. Wide archetypes move more bytes, and mobile entities may require frequent refreshes. Nearby entities in different archetypes remain in separate storage. Neighbor search still needs cell enumeration or an index and distance checks. The dirty-maintenance benchmark compares updates, tracking, classification, sorting, movement, and location repair against explicit full rebuilds; it does not establish a spatial workload speedup.
data.growable-cluster-local-partitions#Growab:
Choose partitions at registration when your workload benefits from moving rows between persistent clusters rather than reordering entire archetypes:
from larecs import World, Filter, SpatialClassifier, SystemContext from larecs.entity import EntityAccessor from std.testing import assert_equal @fieldwise_init struct Cells(SpatialClassifier): comptime Accessor = EntityAccessor[Filter().read[Int]()] def classify(self, entity: Self.Accessor) raises -> UInt64: """Use the nonnegative integer input as the exact cluster key. Args: entity: Borrowed read-only classifier input. Raises: Error: The classifier interface permits errors. Returns: The application cluster identity. """ return UInt64(entity.get[Int]()) def main() raises: """Maintain clusters and acquire exact cluster membership. Raises: Error: If registration, maintenance, or selection fails. """ var world = World[Int]() _ = world.storage.add_entity(7) _ = world.storage.add_entity(9) world.register_spatial_classifier[Filter().read[Int]()]( Cells(), partitioned=True ) world.maintain_spatial() var context = SystemContext(world) var selected = context.select_cluster[Filter().read[Int]()](UInt64(7)) assert_equal(len(selected), 1) selected^.release() Component composition still defines the logical archetype. Each cluster beneath it owns exactly one dense SoA store. Capacity starts at one row and doubles on demand without a fixed row limit. Classifier configuration (for example, cell width) controls cluster population; there is no separate chunk-size option. Separate clusters need not occupy nearby allocations, and partition traversal is not sorted by key.
Creation and component transitions stage rows without calling the classifier. The next explicit maintenance boundary classifies pending inputs and transfers rows into their clusters. Same-composition replacement stays in its physical store until placement is refreshed. Source swap-removal repairs locations. Growing a destination moves its existing column values into larger contiguous allocations. The boundary releases empty cluster/staging row allocations; nonempty stores retain their grown capacity. Queries and ordinary host/device execution traverse every matching physical store, including staged rows. Device calls pack those ranges and scatter writable spans back under the existing transfer and synchronization rules.
context.select_cluster[filter](key) snapshots exact maintained cluster membership, intersected with the component filter across logical archetypes and their cluster stores. Pending maintenance is an error: finish maintenance before capturing membership. The result has the same lock, in-place mutation, scoped lifetime, and reusable kernel calls as other selections. Writes during its lifetime do not change its membership. Release it before maintenance. Empty cluster results still own a lock. This is a key lookup, not a distance or neighbor query.
Partition mode is opt-in and row reordering remains the default. Measure the paired partition benchmark against your entity counts, cell occupancy, component widths, and maintenance cadence. Many sparse cells can cost much more metadata and allocations, and ordinary scans pay traversal/binding cost per cluster store. Active maintenance still copies identity-capacity keys and rebuilds a temporary cluster directory; cluster selection currently scans store metadata. Empty interior slots and directory capacity retain high-water metadata. Structural-heavy frames still perform full classification. See decision 0014 for guarantees and limits.
